Prevalence of AI use in past month increased from 62% to 75% across waves. Any AI use was associated with higher social anxiety (concurrent b = 0.27, P < .001; prospective b = 0.22, P < .001) and depressive symptoms (concurrent b = 0.11, P < .001; prospective b = 0.12, P < .001). Frequency of AI use was associated with loneliness (concurrent b = 0.03, P = .007), social anxiety (concurrent b = 0.08, P < .001; prospective b = 0.07, P < .001) and depressive symptoms (concurrent b = 0.06, P < .001; prospective b = 0.05, P < .001). Factor analyses supported three evaluative dimensions: Emotional Intimacy and Companionship, Nonjudgmental Validation, and Overreliance. Emotional Intimacy and Companionship prospectively predicted greater school loneliness (z = 2.98; P = .003). No internalizing symptom variables prospectively predicted AI evaluations.
Conclusions and Relevance: AI use and evaluations are related to negative mental health outcomes over time for young adolescents. Rapid policy responses and continued longitudinal research are needed to address the public health implications of AI use and companionship during early adolescence.

articles.title: Quantifying Human-AI Synergy
articles.authors: Christoph Riedl; Ben Weidmann
articles.abstract: We introduce a novel Bayesian Item Response Theory framework to quantify human–AI synergy, separating individual and collaborative ability while controlling for task difficulty in interactive settings. Unlike standard static benchmarks, our approach models human–AI performance as a joint process, decomposing additive synergy from non-linear dynamics while capturing both user-specific factors, direct substitution, and moment-to-moment fluctuations. We validate the framework with human–AI benchmark data (n=667) and find significant synergy. We demonstrate that collaboration ability is distinct from individual problem-solving ability. Users better able to infer and adapt to others’ perspectives achieve superior collaborative performance with AI---but not when working alone. Moreover, moment-to-moment fluctuations in perspective taking influence AI response quality, highlighting the role of dynamic user factors in collaboration. By introducing a principled framework to analyze data from human-AI collaboration, interactive benchmarks can better complement current single-task benchmarks and crowd-assessment methods. This work informs the design and training of language models that transcend static prompt benchmarks to achieve adaptive, socially aware collaboration with diverse and dynamic human partners.

articles.title: Psychosocial interventions and health-related quality of life in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Francisca Mena; María Victoria Díaz-Fuenzalida; Stefanella Costa-Cordella; Franco Giraudo Abarca
articles.abstract:
Purpose. To synthesize evidence on the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions in improving health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1D), and to characterize their theoretical foundations, core components, therapeutic targets, and delivery features.
Methods. Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020, prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261349366). Searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, EBSCO, and SCOPUS identified randomized controlled trials published between 2011 and March 2026 evaluating psychosocial interventions in youth (≤18 years) with T1D reporting at least one HRQoL outcome. Two independent reviewers conducted screening, data extraction, and quality appraisal using the NHLBI tool. Interventions were coded using the Theory Coding Scheme. A random-effects meta-analysis (Hedges' g) pooled trials with inactive comparators.
Results. Twelve reports (11 independent RCTs; 2,082 randomized participants) were included. Interventions shared core components (psychoeducation, coping and problem-solving skills, communication and family engagement, and motivational and self-management strategies) despite diverse theoretical traditions. Meta-analysis of five trials (752 participants) demonstrated a small but statistically significant HRQoL improvement compared with inactive controls (Hedges' g = 0.24; 95% CI 0.10–0.38; p = .001; I² = 0%). Improvements in emotional well-being, family functioning, and self-management were more consistent than metabolic gains.
Conclusions. Psychosocial interventions produce reliable though modest HRQoL improvements in children and adolescents with T1D. Theory was used descriptively rather than to test mechanisms. Future trials should designate HRQoL as a primary endpoint and formally test hypothesized mechanisms of change.

articles.title: Triangulating the Cognitive Mechanisms of Naturalistic Human Avoidance Learning
articles.authors: Huaiyu Liu; Josie Linnell; Federico Mancinelli; Tom Beckers; Dominik R Bach
articles.abstract: Learning to avoid harm is essential for wellbeing, and its dysregulation is thought to underlie anxiety-related disorders. To date, there is no generally accepted computational theory of human avoidance learning. A potential reason is the absence of systematic empirical benchmarks capable of distinguishing competing theories. Here, we test 12 canonical and novel associative learning phenomena in a naturalistic avoidance paradigm across six preregistered virtual reality experiments in healthy humans (total N = 599). Our findings converge on three computational principles. First, avoidance learning is predominantly inference-based: participants updated avoidance following signalled US omission and transition structure changes. Second, it reflects cost-benefit integration: spontaneous extinction and retrospective revaluation emerged under naturalistic motor costs, but gave way to residual avoidance when costs were removed. Third, learning about compound cues suggests configural rather than linear feature integration. These principles, and the detailed pattern of findings, can guide the development of candidate computational theories.

articles.title: Local bias and face recognition in autism spectrum disorder: Is there a connection?
articles.authors: Christian Gerlach; Esben Helby; Linnea Brønnum Hansen; Mette Elmose; Ipek Oruc
articles.abstract: It seems well-established that many autistic individuals experience face recognition difficulties. It is also commonly assumed that many autistic individuals exhibit a local bias in visual processing in that they weigh details more than the overall pattern that the details are part of. Given that face recognition seems to depend critically on holistic compared with parts-based processing, this has led to the suggestion that reduced face recognition ability may be a consequence of the altered perceptual processing style in autism. The evidence supporting a direct link is sparse, however, as face recognition and global-local processing are seldomly studied in the same samples. In the present study we thus examined this potential link in a sample of 41 autistic individuals who performed two face recognition experiments as well as Navon’s paradigm which makes it possible to examine different global-local biases directly. In keeping with previous studies, we find that the autistic individuals performed less efficiently than a group of matched non-autistic individuals and that 20% performed at a level comparable with what is seen in developmental prosopagnosia. However, there was no support for group differences in global-local processing with the data being between 3 to 11 times more likely under the hypothesis of no difference between the groups. This suggests that the face recognition difficulties seen in the present sample of autistic individuals are unlikely to reflect a local bias in visual processing.

articles.title: Which Platforms Count? The Diverse Meanings of "Social Media" in the United States
articles.authors: Stephanie Torres-Pantoja; Lisa Rhee; Julian Unkel; Muniba Saleem; Joseph Bayer
articles.abstract:
The effects of using social media platforms remain hotly debated, but insufficient research has
focused on how individuals are defining what social media is. Here, we consider how different
understandings of the term “social media” may influence how people think and talk about social
media experiences and effects. To test this, we asked a nationally representative sample of adults
in the United States (N = 1904) to indicate whether twelve popular platforms are “social media.”
Our results revealed significant variation in the identification of “social media”— with general
agreement that six platforms are social media (Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, Instagram, Snapchat,
and TikTok) and a lack of consensus about the other six (Telegram, Signal, Discord, WhatsApp,
and Messenger, and YouTube). Younger participants were more likely to view four platforms as
social media (Instagram, Snapchat, Twitter, and TikTok), whereas older participants were more
likely to view six platforms as social media (Reddit, YouTube, Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, and
Messenger). Additionally, we examined the correlates of holding broad vs. narrow social media
schemata, finding that individuals with broader schemas perceived hate speech to be more
prevalent on social media. Looking forward, we discuss how the lack of consensus around the
term “social media” may affect how people respond to survey questions about social media, as
well as perceive and converse about their effects and policy implications in society.

articles.title: Above- and Below-Threshold Approaches Reveal Network Enrichment in the Aging Lexicon: Longitudinal Evidence from the Natural Language of 110 Authors
articles.authors: Dasol Jeong; Brendan Johns; Thomas Hills
articles.abstract: This study investigates age-related changes in the mental lexicon using natural language data and network-analytic methods, evaluating whether observed differences reflect cognitive decline or cumulative lifelong learning. Prior research based on free association tasks has suggested that lexical networks become sparser with age; however, such methods may not capture language use in naturalistic contexts. To address this limitation, we analyzed 1,116 English novels written across the lifespan by 110 authors. Contextualized word embeddings were generated using a BERT-based model, and cosine similarity was used to estimate associative strength. Networks were constructed using two complementary thresholding approaches: an above-threshold approach (ATA) retaining only stronger associations and a below-threshold approach (BTA) retaining only weaker associations. In the ATA, age was associated with decreased degree and clustering coefficient and increased average shortest path length, consistent with sparsification. However, when weak-to-moderate associations were included (low-range ATA and BTA), the pattern reversed, indicating denser and more clustered networks with age. Entropy analyses further showed that age-related decreases emerged only when weak associations were excluded. These findings support an enrichment account in which aging expands the underlying associative space, while competitive interference during retrieval yields behaviorally sparser networks.

articles.title: Psychology in 2125: A Developmental Science of Living Sense-Making
articles.authors: Peter J. Marshall
articles.abstract: A century from now, the computational framework at the center of psychology will no longer organize the discipline. As used here, "computational" names a broad information-processing ontology: meaning is specified in advance, rather than generated through the activity, history, and situation of living beings. This assumption fits engineered systems, but it misdescribes living ones. This article argues that three converging shifts are destabilizing that framework. The first undermines the computational account of inheritance: organisms develop through activity within configurations of constraints reconstituted across generations, not through the readout of genetic programs. The second displaces its account of psychological structure: psychological phenomena unfold as trajectories of coordination rather than as stable traits, with reliability and variability arising from the same generative process. The third sharpens the first two: artificial intelligence systems produce fluent performance without embodiment, developmental history, or any stake in the world. This contrast reveals what living organization contributes. The psychology implied by these shifts treats development as foundational, not as a subfield. It understands psychological constructs as patterns of activity that persons sustain over time, and is better positioned to address a century of changing human ecologies. This future psychology will be a developmental science of living sense-making.

articles.title: A Crucial Source of Psychological Certainty in Human Cognition: The Certainty Signature of Central Form
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified. Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty. On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs. The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief. In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts. While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties. In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts. As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept’s central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept’s central form. These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts. Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

articles.title: Neural and behavioural correlates of Theory of Mind reasoning in five year-old children born preterm
articles.authors: Selina Abel; Melissa Thye; Katie Mckinnon; Rebekah Smikle; Jean Skelton; Lorena Jiménez Sánchez; Ray Amir; Gayle Barclay; Charlotte Jardine; Donna McIntyre
articles.abstract:
Abstract 
Behavioural studies suggest atypical or delayed development of “theory of mind” (ToM; our ability to reason about others’ mental states) following preterm birth. Using pre-registered analyses of behavioural and movie-viewing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) metrics of ToM, we tested for a domain-specific impact of preterm birth (24-32 weeks’ gestational age) on theory of mind development at age five years. Preterm-born children (n=52) scored lower than term-born comparators (n=58) on a linguistic behavioural ToM task, but this difference was primarily driven by differences in receptive language. Neurally, preterm-born children (n=30) had qualitatively similar responses in brain regions that support ToM reasoning to a short movie to term-born comparators (n=46), as characterised by four neural metrics; responses to one scene differed as a function of gestational age. Using intersubject correlation analyses, we found that preterm-born children’s ToM network responses were more heterogenous than term-born children’s responses; however individual preterm-born children’s responses most resembled those observed in same-age term-born children, relative to younger children or other preterm-born children. Taken together, preterm birth does not appear to preclude broadly similar functional development in ToM brain regions by age five years.

articles.title: An Integrative Multidimensional-Motivational-Model of Parent Engagement and Disaffection in Child Education
articles.authors: Richard Anthony Inman; Carina Mota Santos; Sofia Mendes
articles.abstract: Schools and education policymakers have long recognized the importance of parents’ contributions to children’s learning, academic success, and healthy socioemotional development. Yet the widely used construct parent engagement is conceptually diffuse, with limited agreement about its defining features, its distinction from related constructs such as parent involvement, and the processes through which it develops and influences children. To address these limitations, we propose an Integrative Multidimensional Motivational Model of Parent Engagement and Disaffection in Child Education. The model integrates and builds on insights from current theories of parent involvement and engagement, as well as various engagement models from educational, organizational, and environmental psychology literatures. It takes a ‘self-in-role’ perspective, considering how parents’ function in relation to two distinct education-related roles: the parent-as-coeducator role and the parent-as-school-community-member role. For each role, the model distinguishes engagement from disaffection as distinct states of functioning; disaffection conceptualized not merely as the absence of engagement, but as the presence of specific maladaptive processes and states. Engagement and disaffection are further conceptualized as multidimensional psychological phenomena that capture the quality of parents’ experience and enactment of each role with distinct emotional, cognitive, and behavioral (conative) components. The model also frames parent engagement and disaffection as malleable context-dependent states arising from parents’ interactions with people, objects and symbols in their surrounding contexts. These contextual conditions are expected to shape parents’ engagement and disaffection through their appraisals of competence, autonomy, and relatedness while enacting each role. In turn, the model hypothesizes that parent engagement and disaffection influence children by shaping the relational, motivational, and educational conditions through which children’s own psychological needs and academic functioning are supported or undermined. We close the article by discussing the theoretical and applied implications of the proposed model and its potential for advancing the field of parent engagement.

articles.title: The emergence and maturation of the infant alpha peak reflect a transition from transient bursts to sustained oscillations
articles.authors: Josué Rico-Picó; Haleigh M. Brown; Kathryn N. Gray; Sonya V. Troller-Renfree
articles.abstract: The emergence of the alpha peak is a milestone in brain development. For decades, metrics commonly used to quantify alpha have collapsed its temporal dimension, which can obscure the course of alpha development when the rhythm is not yet sustained. Here, we leveraged over 600 resting EEG recordings from 207 children aged 1–48 months to chart alpha development through its rhythmic structure and transient recruitment (bursts) and related these time-resolved measures to traditional measures of alpha from the power spectrum. We show that early alpha (1 to 12 months) depended largely on transient bursts. As alpha became more rhythmic with age, alpha power relied progressively less on burst activity. These findings indicate that the development of the alpha peak may reflect a fundamental shift from a transient to a more sustained rhythm. Time-resolved metrics are therefore essential for characterizing alpha accurately in early development.

articles.title: Comparing Counterspeech by Moderators, Bots, and Community: Technique Effects and Gender-Specific Source Effects on Perceived Harmfulness
articles.authors: Holger Heppner; Udo Seelmeyer; Birte Schiffhauer
articles.abstract: This study examined the effectiveness of different counterspeech techniques and the influence of counterspeech source on reducing perceived harmfulness of harmful online comments. In a preregistered experiment (N = 272), participants viewed harmful comments about a controversial topic paired with counterspeech varying in technique (Denouncing, Appealing to Compassion, Presenting Facts, Redirecting) and source (Moderator, Bot, Community Note). Perceived harmfulness was measured using the newly developed Perceived Harmfulness Scale (PHS), encompassing Emotional Distress, Feeling of Threat, Social Exclusion, and Discourse Disruption. Three of four techniques – Appealing to Compassion, Presenting Facts, and Redirecting – demonstrated equal effectiveness in reducing perceived harmfulness of a harmful comment, while Denouncing was ineffective. At the aggregate level, counterspeech source had no main effect. However, exploratory analyses revealed a crossover interaction between source and participant gender: bot-based and moderator-based counterspeech reduced perceived harmfulness only for male participants, while for female participants only community-based counterspeech was effective. For women, bot-based counterspeech was even counterproductive. These findings suggest that attention management may be more effective than norm activation in reducing perceived harmfulness, and that one-size-fits-all approaches to content moderation may inadvertently fail specific user groups. Platforms may benefit from diversified moderation strategies combining automated detection with community-based responses to address diverse user needs.

articles.title: Stimulation Uncertainty Reveals Distinct Mechanisms of Sensation Seeking and Impulsivity
articles.authors: Ern Wong; Tobias U. Hauser; Aswath Chandrasekaran; Pietro Pietrini; Charley M Wu
articles.abstract: Sensation-seeking is often described as a tendency to pursue novel and stimulating experiences, yet such options are often uncertain as well. This creates a central ambiguity where choices that appear to reflect attraction to stimulation may instead reflect tolerance of uncertain outcomes, or an interaction between the two. Across two experiments, we tested how expected stimulation and stimulation uncertainty shape reward-guided choice. A reanalysis of a previous operant sensation-seeking dataset suggests that stimulation uncertainty explained behaviour better than expected stimulation. Subsequently, we conducted a preregistered online experiment to investigate the joint effects of expected stimulation and stimulation uncertainty and to compare their respective associations with sensation-seeking and impulsivity. Our results indicate that higher sensation-seeking was associated with broader stochastic sampling and lower reward performance, but this was not reducible to random choice or uncertainty tolerance alone. Instead, uncertainty weighting depended on the value assigned to expected stimulation. This profile differed from impulsivity, suggesting that the two traits shape choice through distinct computational routes. By separating expected stimulation from uncertainty, these findings refine accounts of exploratory choice by showing that sensation-seeking shapes not only how much people sample uncertain options, but how stimulation value and uncertainty are jointly weighted during choice.

articles.title: Leveling Up Motor Function: A Systematic Review of Adaptive Motor Difficulty and Reinforcement Schemes in Commercial and Research Video Games
articles.authors: Gal Raz; Shira Badusa; Romi Sion; Alexis Mitelpunkt
articles.abstract:
Video games, by providing dense practice of goal-directed motor actions with immediate and salient feedback, have drawn growing interest in motor learning and rehabilitation research. Yet most studies do not specify which game design mechanisms drive improvement—a gap that may hinder our ability to understand and exploit the unique potential of video games for motor learning.

To address this, we propose a refined taxonomy of adaptive difficulty and reinforcement (AD&R) schemes comprising three mechanisms: Skill-Based Progression (SBP; the incremental adjustment of game difficulty), Target Manipulation Boosting (TMB; powering-up the player's impact on targets), and Control Boosting (CB; amplifying virtual movement relative to physical input). We discuss the neuroscientific features of these distinct schemes in the context of reinforcement learning.

Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we systematically reviewed the prevalence of these schemes across commercial video games (n=162), clinical studies (n=287), and non-clinical studies (n=98) published between 2020 and 2024. Using a rigorously validated Large Language Model coding pipeline, our analysis (n=547) revealed that all three AD&R schemes are underrepresented in games employed in academic research compared to commercial games. Specifically, TMB and CB are nearly absent in research, showing 67.9% prevalence in commercial games compared to 1.4% in clinical and 2.1% in non-clinical games for TMB, and 58.6% compared to 1.4% and 3.1% for CB.

Ultimately, this study demonstrates that academic research paradigms significantly underutilize performance-amplifying game mechanics. Integrating TMB and CB into neurorehabilitation protocols provides an actionable framework to optimize motor skill transfer, emotional engagement, and user agency.

articles.title: Prevalence of Emotional and Relational Engagement with AI and Their Associations with Psychosocial Adjustment among College Students
articles.authors: Huiguang Ren; Chuqi Chen; Fangfang Tian; Junsheng Liu
articles.abstract: Although growing evidence suggests that some individuals use generative artificial intelligence (GAI) for emotional support and companionship, little is known about how prevalent these experiences are, who is most likely to report them, and how they relate to psychosocial adjustment. The present study addressed these questions using a regionally representative sample of 1,406 university students from 26 universities in Shanghai, China (Mage = 18.98 years, SD = 1.25, 59.7% female). Results indicated that most participants primarily viewed AI as a functional tool, whereas emotionally meaningful engagement remained relatively uncommon. Nevertheless, approximately one in seven participants reported moderate to high levels of personal disclosure or emotional attachment to AI. Emotional and relational engagement with AI was more common among individuals reporting greater interpersonal vulnerabilities and lower relational resources. Different forms of AI engagement also showed distinct patterns of association with psychosocial adjustment. Assistance-oriented engagement was associated with more positive interpersonal orientations, whereas more emotionally intensive forms of engagement were associated with poorer psychosocial adjustment. These findings suggest that emotional engagement with AI is already a meaningful experience for a subset of young adults and is embedded within broader patterns of interpersonal functioning and psychosocial adjustment.

articles.title: Cognitive Functioning is Better on Computers than on Smartphones:  A Multilevel Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Shir Etgar; Niall Bolger
articles.abstract: People use computers and smartphones interchangeably for a wide range of tasks, yet it remains unclear whether both devices support cognitive functioning equally well. So far, the answer to this question comes from many fragmented findings across various fields of research, sometimes pointing in opposite directions, making it difficult to draw general conclusions. To investigate the overall effect of device type on cognitive functioning, we conducted a multilevel meta-analysis of the literature, with three levels of analysis (3680 participants within 69 studies within 18 papers). Studies were included if they measured actual cognitive functioning in a randomized experimental design. We found an overall effect of device type, with cognitive functioning better when tasks were completed on computers than on smartphones. The effect was not moderated by device ownership, study design (between/within), study environment (online/laboratory), or year of publication. We discuss several potential explanations for this effect and recommend tailoring tasks to devices to enhance cognitive functioning in the digital era.

articles.title: The RFT Perspective Taking Protocol has very poor reliability and convergent validity with other measures of perspective taking, empathy, and theory of mind: A jingle assessment
articles.authors: Ian Hussey; Malte Elson
articles.abstract: Relational Frame Theory (RFT) conceptualises perspective taking and related constructs of empathy, theory of mind, and false-belief understanding in terms of deictic relational responding. RFT's Perspective Taking Protocol was originally developed to assess and train these relational repertoires, and increasingly became used to measure individual differences in perspective taking in adult and clinical samples. This slippage was recently raised as a concern regarding its appropriate use: the latter presupposes that PTP scores are reliable and valid measure of a perspective-taking trait, yet these properties have rarely been tested. This puts it at risk of jingle fallacy: the assumption similarly named measures measure similar things. We administered a 9-item PTP to 134 adults online, retesting 98 participants after a 10-day interval, alongside established self-report and behavioural measures of perspective taking, empathy, and theory of mind. The PTP showed poor internal consistency (α = .40, 95% CI [.24, .54]) and test–retest reliability indistinguishable from zero (ICC2,1 = .08, 95% CI [−.12, .27]); its trial-type subscales did not cohere (subscale correlations from r = -.08 to .22); and it was essentially uncorrelated with existing measures even after disattenuating for unreliability. A meta-analysis demonstrated that the PTP is on average unrelated to other measures (r = .01, disattenuated r = .03) whereas those measures are generally associated with one another (r = .28, disattenuated r = .35). Results question whether the PTP should be used as a measure of individual differences in perspective taking; naming it a perspective-taking measure may represent a jingle fallacy.

articles.title: Habit learning and expression as stable traits
articles.authors: Pablo Martínez-López; José Juan León; Francisco Garre-Frutos; Antonio Vázquez-Millán; Sara Molinero; Tamara Giménez-Fernández; Miguel A. Vadillo; David Luque
articles.abstract: Individual differences in the capacity to learn and control habits are central to current models of psychopathology, which assume an overreliance on habit behavior in transdiagnostic compulsivity. However, whether these tendencies reflect stable, trait-like cognitive processes remains unclear. We examined the temporal stability of individual differences in habit learning and expression. Across two preregistered experiments, we assessed stimulus–response habits using the same stimuli after one day or different stimuli after four months. Evidence for stable individual differences in habit commissions was strong and comparable across experiments, indicating trait-like habit learning and expression. Improvements in response time across learning were stable and correlated with habits, suggesting an early trait-like index of habitualization. Stable processes of habit formation were reflected during both habit acquisition and expression.

articles.title: Conditional Associations Between HEXACO Personality Traits and NEET Status in Young Adults
articles.authors: Martina Pastorelli; Anna Laura Vlad; maria esposito; Andrea Ceschi; Riccardo Sartori; Michele Scandola
articles.abstract:
Young people classified as NEET (Not in Employment, Education, or Training) represent a heterogeneous population whose educational and occupational disengagement may be shaped by the interplay between personality traits, psychological resources, and contextual conditions. Although previous research has examined several risk factors associated with NEET status, evidence on the role of personality and its interaction with self-regulatory and psychosocial resources remains limited. 

This study examined the psychological and sociodemographic correlates of NEET status in a sample of 254 young adults, including 75 NEET and 179 non-NEET participants. HEXACO personality dimensions, perceived employability, self-directed learning, future-oriented beliefs, mental health, perceived social support, education, age, and sex were assessed. Principal component analysis identified three broader dimensions: Strategic Future-Oriented Mindset, Mental Health, and Social Support. A binomial regression model showed that NEET status was associated with a complex pattern of conditional effects rather than with isolated personality traits. Strategic Future-Oriented Mindset was negatively associated with NEET status particularly at low and average levels of Honesty–Humility. Social Support was associated with a lower probability of being NEET mainly among individuals high in Extraversion. Emotionality emerged as the most stable personality-related risk factor, whereas education was negatively associated with NEET status and moderated the role of specific personality dimensions. 

These findings suggest that NEET status should be understood through a person-context framework in which personality traits interact with psychological resources and sociodemographic conditions. Interventions aimed at supporting young people at risk of educational and occupational disengagement should therefore move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches and strengthen strategic future-oriented self-regulation, interpersonal learning, emotional regulation, and the effective activation of social support.

articles.title: Laughing Together Influences Neural Synchrony in Child Peers: An fNIRS Hyperscanning Study
articles.authors: Verena Schäfer; Carolina Pletti; Stefanie Hoehl
articles.abstract: Shared laughter, a salient social cue in peer interactions, promotes bonding, liking and prosociality. Recent theoretical accounts on the neural dynamics of social interaction propose that rhythmic communicative signals, such as laughter, may foster neural synchrony by aligning brain activities between interacting partners, facilitating mutual understanding and social bonding. Here, we test whether neural synchrony mediates the positive social effects of laughing together in child peer dyads. We used fNIRS hyperscanning to measure neural synchrony in 5-year-old dyads (n = 196; 98 pairs) randomly assigned to a laughter condition (funny animal videos) or a control condition (neutral videos). Inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and temporoparietal junction (TPJ) activity was recorded both during the video manipulation and during a subsequent 5-minute free-play session, and quantified with Wavelet Transform Coherence. Laughter behavior was annotated, bonding indexed by body proximity, prosociality with a sticker sharing task, and liking with smiley scales. Hypotheses were tested with Bayesian models. Compared with controls, children in the laughter condition showed higher neural synchrony while co-watching the videos. During free play, after the manipulation, left-hemisphere synchrony was greater in the control group. Exploratory findings showed that more laughter was linked to stronger bonding and prosociality. We did not find support for a mediation between laughter, neural synchrony and social outcomes. In summary, we show that neural synchrony among children changes with shared laughter. By revealing condition-specific and region-specific effects across time, this study highlights the dynamic nature of neural synchrony processes in child peer interactions.

articles.title: Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater! Why "preregistration" is still a useful term: Commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)
articles.authors: Priya Silverstein; Lisa Spitzer; Lukas Wallrich; Josefina Weinerova
articles.abstract: This is a commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025), published in Avances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science (AMPPS). As per AMPPS submission guidelines, no abstract is included for commentaries.

articles.title: Impairment in the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology
articles.authors: Christopher James Hopwood; Colin G. DeYoung; Stephen Aita; Elizabeth Bell; Stephen D Benning; Marina Bornovalova; Lee Anna Clark; Nicholas R Eaton; Omid V. Ebrahimi; Darren Haywood
articles.abstract:
The purpose of this paper is to define and describe impairment from the perspective of the
Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP). This work is intended to establish a
foundation for the development of a system for assessing impairment to complement HiTOP
measures of psychopathology. We define impairment as the direct or indirect impact of
psychopathology that is not itself part of psychopathology, involving (a) difficulty achieving
important and reasonable personal goals and/or (b) direct or indirect interference with the goals
of others. We articulate seven specific assessment features of a HiTOP-optimal impairment
measurement approach and, having found no existing measures with all seven features in a
review of the literature, sketch a prototype approach using a case example and outline a plan
for generating a suite of tools for assessing impairment from a HiTOP perspective.

articles.title: Participation Effects in Ecological Momentary Assessment Research: A Taxonomy and Call to Action
articles.authors: Eveline Gieles; Leonie V. D. E. Vogelsmeier; Joran Jongerling; Tom Smeets; Egon Dejonckheere
articles.abstract:
Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) is often praised for its ecological validity, under the assumption that change observed in EMA data reflects change in the underlying constructs, independent of study participation. However, participation itself may threaten ecological validity as participants’ involvement in an EMA study may already alter their experiences, behavior or responses. Existing research on such participation effects has primarily documented their occurrence rather than explained the mechanisms through which they arise. To advance this understanding, we developed a taxonomy of potential sources of (measurement-induced) change in EMA data. This taxonomy includes increased reflection on assessed constructs (i.e., measurement reactivity), alterations to daily routines (i.e., measurement interference), shifts in how participants interpret items or response scales (i.e., reconceptualization or recalibration), practice in gauging internal states (i.e., improved introspection), and declining participant engagement (i.e., heightened careless responding or reduced compliance). Identifying these distinct sources of change highlights the need for systematic investigation of their impact and the development of targeted mitigation strategies. We therefore outline a research agenda focusing on assessing and experimentally manipulating each source of measurement-induced change in isolation. In sum, this paper aims to initiate a collective effort among EMA researchers to clarify the mechanisms by which study participation shapes data, and to safeguard EMA’s promise of ecological validity. 

Keywords: experience sampling methodology, measurement reactivity, (ecological) validity, response shifts, careless or insufficient effort responding

articles.title: Two-Axis Institutional Thoughtlessness in Japanese Euthanasia Case Law: A Computational Discourse Analysis of 113 Judgments, 1964–2024
articles.authors: Masahiro Sadamura; Tomoya Mukai; Tomohiro Ioku; Eiichiro Watamura
articles.abstract:
Background: Japan lacks statutory legislation for euthanasia, physician-assisted suicide, or treatment withdrawal; case law from the 1962 Nagoya Yamauchi judgment through the 1995 Tokai University four-criteria framework, the 2009 Kawasaki Supreme Court decision, and the 2024 Kyoto ALS convictions has established the de facto normative criteria.

Methods: We present the first systematic computational analysis of Japanese euthanasia-related judicial discourse (N = 113 bibliographically verified judgments, 1964–2024; sensitivity N = 119) using a 14-layer robustness hierarchy that pairs lexicon-based modelling with Tohoku-BERT v3 fine-tuning, leave-one-out sensitivity, a scramble-label negative control, and three-LLM inter-model reliability.

Results: Relative to the three-factor public benchmark from Watamura, Hunt, and Ioku (2026, Ethics & Behavior; Euthanasia Attitude Scale, Tordella and Neutens 1979; analytic N = 890), judicial discourse shows between-scale standardized discrepancies (not within-population Cohen's d) of −3.21 on openness-to-ending-life, −4.26 on dignified self-determination, and +1.49 on family-and-social-order, under primary scaling convention pooled-SD, supported under three of four conventions and across all 113 leave-one-out drops.

Conclusions: The pattern admits an institutional-thoughtlessness two-axis reading (judicial discourse de-emphasizes both patient autonomy and the broad openness-to-ending-life construct that F1 captures, of which suffering-termination is one component) and an institutional-prudence counter-reading anchored in Japanese communitarian bioethics; Stage 2 is designed to adjudicate.

articles.title: Changes in and Stability of Well-Being During Adolescence:  A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Studies Over Two Decades
articles.authors: Yi-Jhen Wu; Michael Becker; Ronny Scherer
articles.abstract: In this meta-analytic review, we examine the development of well-being during adolescence by synthesizing mean-level changes and rank-order stability in longitudinal studies. We conceptualize well-being as a multidimensional construct that includes hedonic well-being, eudaimonic well-being, and quality of life. To compute effect sizes, we used the standardized mean change d per year and test-retest correlations adjusted for measurement error. Analyses of the mean-level change were based on 502 effect sizes from a total of 551,009 adolescents. Analyses of the rank-order stability were based on 427 effect sizes from a total of 515,081 adolescents. The results showed that well-being declines every year (d ̅_year = −.03) and the cumulative decline during adolescence is d= -.27. The rank-order stability is high (r ̅ = .62). Only the linear function of age was positively related to rank-order stability. Moderator analyses showed that the findings for mean-level changes and rank-order stability were consistent across gender, birth cohort, ethnicity, economic development of the country, concepts of well-being, positive and negative aspects of well-being, and the quality of studies. Time interval length was negatively associated with rank-order stability. The subgroup analysis of the positive and negative aspects of well-being revealed that younger generations born after 2000 are more likely to experience greater declines in well-being. In sum, well-being tends to decline during adolescence, yet well-being is stable. These findings provide a clear and precise picture of the changes in well-being and the stability of well-being during adolescence.

articles.title: Dynamical Fit Index Cutoffs for Gaussian Graphical Models
articles.authors: Xinkai Du; Sacha Epskamp
articles.abstract:
As exploratory network research continues to grow, there is heightened demand for confirmatory network analysis that can validate replicability and examine hypotheses. The quality of confirmatory testing depends critically on reliable fit index cutoffs that control type I and type II errors during hypothesis testing. However, conventional cutoffs developed by Hu and Bentler (1999; HB cutoffs) are inflexible and are vulnerable to sample and model characteristics, creating a demand for more flexible dynamic fit index (DFI) cutoffs that can be adapted to researchers’ specific designs. In this study, we attempted to develop a DFI algorithm for Gaussian graphical models, a widely implemented network model, and compared the performance of DFI cutoffs with HB cutoffs
in terms of their specificity and sensitivity to misspecifications. In simulation studies based on both synthetic and empirical networks, DFI provided more flexible cutoffs with a transparent, fixed power/specificity to detect correctly specified models and was often more sensitive to misspecifications, especially in empirical networks. The DFI for network models provides a more reliable and flexible criterion for confirmatory network analysis, thereby marking an essential advancement in theory and hypothesis testing in network research. The algorithm has been implemented in an open-source, user-friendly R package, netDFI.

articles.title: The Price of Prediction: Robust False Memories in Naturalistic Contexts
articles.authors: Mahveen Salman Mubarak; Keisuke Fukuda
articles.abstract: The human brain predicts incoming visual events to make sense of the world in real time. While prior work has shown that explicit predictions can induce false memories of the predicted event using artificial and decontextualized stimuli, whether these distortions generalize to naturalistic settings remains unknown. To test this, participants viewed first-person videos of everyday events, that paused midway to prompt predictions about what would happen next, followed by the actual outcome. Predictions were either confirmed by the predicted event occurring, directly rebutted by a different event occurring, or left unresolved with no outcome shown. Across four experiments, we show that merely generating a prediction is sufficient to induce a false memory of the predicted event in a rich, naturalistic context, even when that prediction is directly rebutted. This effect persisted regardless of whether participants were explicitly instructed to remember the actual outcome and was, in fact, amplified under incident encoding. Strikingly, these false memories not only survived a 24-hour delay but became stronger in the absence of feedback, as veridical memories deteriorated. Together, these findings demonstrate the strong influence of predictions on what we remember, underlining the powerful role of expectations in shaping episodic memories even under ecologically valid conditions.

articles.title: Judging My-side versus Thy-side: Meta-Forecasting Accuracy Predicts Forecasting Accuracy in the Political Domain
articles.authors: Pearlyn Ng; Alexander C. Walker; Robert N. Collins; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Harrison Oakes; Heather Walker; David R. Mandel
articles.abstract: Forecasting research has capitalized on performance-related individual difference measures to improve forecasting accuracy by indicating who is likely a better forecaster, but few studies have examined how socially-relevant factors influence forecasting accuracy. In two experiments (N = 2,921), we examined how accurately participants estimated the average forecasts of political ingroups and outgroups (meta-forecasts). We tested whether these meta-forecasts predicted participants’ forecasts of the actual outcomes. We found that participants were better at predicting the forecasts of ingroups than of outgroups on group-relevant topics (politics in our study), but not on group-adjacent (i.e, non-political) topics. While meta-forecasting accuracy was predictive of forecasting accuracy, in general, ingroup meta-forecasts on group-relevant topics were particularly good at predicting forecasting accuracy on the topics themselves. Moreover, this did not depend on participants’ political affiliation. Meta-forecasts added indicative value regarding forecasting accuracy above and beyond numeracy and an actively open-minded thinking style.

articles.title: Mental Well-Being and Anxiety Among Ready-Made Garment Workers in Gazipur, Bangladesh: A Gender-Based Cross-Sectional Study
articles.authors: Olima Akter Mim; Sharof Shahrul Hoque
articles.abstract:
The ready-made garment (RMG) industry is a major contributor to Bangladesh’s economy,
employing millions of workers under often stressful conditions. Despite its economic
importance, limited research has examined the mental well-being and anxiety of this workforce,
particularly regarding gender differences. This cross-sectional study investigated the relationship
between mental well-being and anxiety among male and female garment workers in Gazipur,
Bangladesh. A total of 180 participants (90 males, 90 females), aged 18–30 years (M = 24), were
recruited through purposive sampling. The Bangla-adapted Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-
Being Scale and Anxiety Scale were administered, and descriptive and inferential analyses were
conducted. Results indicated that male workers reported higher mean mental well-being scores
(M = 53.51, SD = 8.3) than female workers (M = 49.91, SD = 10.7), which is statistically
significant {t(178) = 2.50, p = 0.013}. Mean anxiety scores were 44.08 (SD = 13.08) for males
and 41.57 (SD = 15.4) for females, with no significant gender difference { t(178) = 1.18, p =
0.240}. Overall, anxiety and mental well-being were negatively correlated (r = −0.31, p < 0.01),
suggesting that higher mental well-being is associated with lower anxiety.

articles.title: Stress, somatic symptoms, and stress reduction methods: A dynamic network approach
articles.authors: Duanmu Chuanyun; Sacha Epskamp
articles.abstract: Conceptualizing psychological stress as a dynamic network of causally connected symptoms could provide valuable insight into its relationships with somatic health issues. This may also provide insight into the functioning and maintenance of chronic stress, along with how stress reduction methods function. Intensive longitudinal data were collected from 46 university students through a mobile app. Participants completed 5 surveys at fixed 3-hour intervals every day for 7 days. In the survey, stress symptom questions were adapted from the Perceived Stress Scale (Lee, 2012) and somatic symptom questions from the DSM-5, while stress reduction questions were newly created for this study. Multilevel vector autoregression was then used to produce temporal and contemporaneous networks. In the temporal network, feedback loops among cognitive psychological symptoms were observed, which predicted other psychological symptoms, and some somatic symptoms. In the contemporaneous network, positive psychological symptoms, negative psychological symptoms, and somatic symptoms were found to cluster together. Correlations between some psychological and somatic symptoms were also observed. Stress reduction methods did not display much effect on other variables in either network. A potential activation pathway for chronic stress was observed. Relationships between psychological and physical stress symptoms may occur rapidly. However, numerous limitations prevent the causal interpretability of results.

articles.title: How Significant Others Shape Human Development: Implications for Significant Other AI
articles.authors: Sung Park; Mayu Koike; Yuri Oki; Soyoung Jung; Seohyun Cho
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly evolving from a task-oriented tool into a long-term relational partner. While prior Human-AI relationship research has primarily examined individual relational constructs such as trust, attachment, empathy, and companionship, relatively little is known about the broader developmental functions that psychologically significant relationships serve in people's lives. Building upon the recently proposed Significant Other AI (SO-AI) Measurement Framework, we conducted the first empirical investigation of how significant others influence human development and how contemporary AI systems compare across these relational functions. Using a mixed-methods design, 210 participants completed the SO-AI Questionnaire, which combined quantitative evaluations of human significant others and AI with qualitative narratives describing the influence of significant others. Quantitative analyses showed that human significant others were perceived significantly more positively than AI across all seven relational dimensions. However, AI demonstrated comparable consultation preferences in situations involving embarrassment, privacy, and social hesitation. Thematic analysis identified seven developmental functions of significant others, including emotional support, relational security, self-confidence, resilience, values and perspective change, communication competence, and internalized guidance. We propose a developmental pathway illustrating how repeated relational experiences foster long-term psychological development and gradually become internalized as enduring psychological guidance. We extend the original SO-AI concept by introducing Developmental SO-AI, a perspective that conceptualizes future relational AI as continuously evolving alongside users through sustained interaction. This work provides the first empirical validation of the SO-AI Measurement Framework and offers theoretical and practical implications for designing relational AI that supports long-term psychological development.

articles.title: The Development of Sensitivity to Automatic Behavior
articles.authors: Ilona Bass; Elizabeth Bonawitz; Tomer David Ullman
articles.abstract: People’s behavior can be roughly categorized into two modes: reflective and thoughtful, or automatic and rote. Past work on Theory of Mind has focused on how children reason about the first category of behavior. But do children also notice when other people are acting in an automatic way? And if so, when might this matter? This paper examined 5- to 10-year-old children’s reasoning about others’ rote behavior, mainly focusing on the consequences of this inference in teaching contexts (N = 660 across four studies, 327 girls; data collected online from U.S.-based children between May 2022 and December 2024). Children’s sensitivity to apparent rote behavior increased with development, with more consistent inferences emerging around age 7. Rote behavior was also associated with worse teaching. These results indicate when and how reasoning about automatic behavior matters to children’s perception of others, and suggest novel extensions to models of Theory of Mind.

articles.title: Crowdstorming You Can Trust? Assessing the Reliability of Crowdsourced Ideation and Prioritization
articles.authors: Younes JEDDI; Maurice Balick; Emile Servan-Schreiber
articles.abstract: Asking crowds of stakeholders to generate and prioritize ideas has become commonplace, from citizen assemblies to corporate open-innovation challenges. Although the reliability of the results of such consultations is taken for granted, their consistency across independent groups has received little empirical attention, largely because such processes are typically one-off events that cannot easily be repeated. In this exploratory study, we introduce the concept of parallel-crowds reliability, the consistency of outcomes when the same collective intelligence process is applied to the same problem by different but demographically equivalent crowds, and we provide an initial empirical test of it. Two separate but equivalent groups of MBA students in the same course were asked to independently propose and prioritize ideas to improve their MBA program, with the same decision-maker curating and selecting winning ideas in both groups. We assess reliability at three successive stages using semantic similarity measures based on two independent embedding models. We find that the two groups independently proposed semantically similar ideas, with convergence concentrated among valuable ideas and divergence among poor ones. They also prioritized similar ideas similarly, enabling the decision maker to select similar sets of winning ideas. Given the single-domain design, we frame these results as an initial evidence base for future investigations.

articles.title: Mental Health Benchmarks for Large Language Models: A Systematic Scoping Review
articles.authors: Matthew Flathers; Phuong Anh Hue Nguyen; Jill Noorily; Julian Herpertz; Sam Cong; Elombe Calvert; Allison Oh; Sunnie Li; Erlend Lane; Kathryn Taylor Ledley
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for mental health support, yet standards for evaluating their safety and competence remain unsettled. Benchmarks, standardized tests with predetermined scoring criteria, are the most common evaluation approach, but this landscape has not been systematically mapped. In this systematic scoping review, we searched four databases, machine-learning repositories, and grey literature through February 2026 and identified 173 publicly available mental health benchmarks for LLMs, extracting 48 fields covering what each benchmark measures, how it was constructed, and how performance is evaluated. The field has grown sharply recently, with more than 70% of benchmarks appearing in 2024 or later, but remains shaped by data availability rather than clinical relevance. Risk and safety, diagnosis, and therapeutic skills dominate, while bias and stigma are nearly absent. Social media and LLM-simulated content are the leading data sources, and data drawn from clinical care are rare. Ethical and methodological safeguards, including ethics review, demographic reporting, human baselines, and hidden test sets, were reported infrequently. Nearly half of the benchmarks involve an LLM in generating items, annotating labels, or judging outputs, a share that reached 90% of new releases by 2026. Shared reporting standards, clinically grounded data, and stronger safeguards are needed for benchmark scores to support claims about safety and clinical capability in mental health care.

articles.title: Does Authenticity Matter in Humor Appreciation?
articles.authors: Drew Gorenz; Norbert Schwarz
articles.abstract: Does authenticity matter in a domain where one’s words and persona aren’t meant to be taken at face value? People often say “I’m just joking” to mean “Don’t take my words or actions literally.” To date, little is known about the role of authenticity in humor appreciation. To explore this question, we used audio recordings of comedic stories told by standup comedians (Experiments 1-3), text-only comedic stories (Experiments 4 & 6), and text-only observational jokes (Experiment 5) as comedic materials. We manipulated perceptions of authenticity by alleging the comedian prioritizes authentic self-expression (vs. pleasing their audience) (Experiment 1), performs because they love performing (vs. for fame and money) (Experiment 2), tells jokes that are based on real, personal (vs. fictional, imagined) experiences (Experiments 3 & 6), or wrote their own jokes (vs. used another human writer or AI) (Experiments 4-5). Across all studies, people evaluated the allegedly authentic jokes as funnier and expressed greater interest in following or sharing the comedian’s work.

articles.title: Routine safety narratives reveal dynamic traces of organisational climate
articles.authors: Michael Alan Rosen; Molly Kilcullen; Yuxin Zhu
articles.abstract: ‘Safety climate’ refers to the shared attitudes about safety within an organisation. While traditionally measured via self-report surveys, it can now be measured by analysing the language in written incident reports. Using large-language model-based machine text analysis, we examined whether text-derived measures predict future safety outcomes in four high-risk industries (i.e., rail, nuclear, mining and aviation) and found that safety climate operates through two distinct pathways. First, stronger safety climate predicts less harm and operational failures, suggesting a preventative effect. Second, a stronger safety climate predicts more formal reporting and documentation, reflecting a culture in which workers feel comfortable raising concerns. To ensure these findings were not analytical artefacts, we tested 810 reasonable variations of each analysis using held-out data for validation. Some findings proved robust across all approaches; others depended on specific methodological decisions. This framework demonstrates how organisations can use large-language model-based text analysis to track safety culture dynamically, while validating these measures against real-world outcomes.

articles.title: Passive Digital Phenotyping for Identifying Dynamic Symptom Patterns: Toward Precision Monitoring in Psychiatry
articles.authors: Rony Kapel Lev-ari; Christian A. Webb; Doron Amsalem; Annika C. Sweetland; Yuval Neria; Milton Wainberg
articles.abstract:
Abstract:
Background:
Mental health symptoms fluctuate over short timeframes, yet clinical assessment typically relies on infrequent self-report, limiting the ability to capture dynamic symptom patterns. Passive digital phenotyping enables continuous, low-burden monitoring of behavioral signals associated with mental health, but the clinical meaning of short-term passive symptom trajectories remains poorly understood. Precision psychiatry calls for approaches that enable individualized characterization of symptom trajectories to inform stratified and responsive treatment.
Methods:
Anonymized passive digital phenotyping data from 13,098 adults were analyzed using a smartphone application that generated daily Mental Health Similarity Scores (MHSS) for depression, anxiety, stress, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) across seven consecutive days, approximating the interval between routine weekly clinical assessments, using validated machine-learning models anchored to standard clinical questionnaires. Latent class growth analyses identified short-term trajectories, and bivariate models examined depression-anxiety co-fluctuation and stratification by depression burden.
Results:
Depression and anxiety demonstrated heterogeneous short-term trajectories, including stable low, stable high and fluctuating patterns, suggesting distinct short-term symptom dynamics. In contrast, stress and ADHD were largely stable over time. Bivariate analyses identified four synchronized depression-anxiety trajectory classes, ranging from stable low to fluctuating co-occurring profiles. Higher depression was associated with persistently elevated and less variable anxiety patterns.
Conclusions:
Passive digital phenotyping offers a scalable, low-burden approach for continuous symptom monitoring, enabling identification of dynamic risk and resilience profiles at the individual level. Trajectory-based digital phenotypes may support precision psychiatry by informing patient stratification, early detection of symptom change, and more adaptive and personalized approaches to monitoring and intervention.

Key Words: Passive digital phenotyping; Mental health; Precision Psychiatry

articles.title: When ‘Us’ Matters Less: Social Identity Complexity and Reduced Ingroup Favoritism in Stereotyping
articles.authors: Trystan Loustau; Gandalf Nicolas
articles.abstract: How do people’s own identity structures shape the way they stereotype others? Across two preregistered experiments using a free-response stereotyping task and valence analysis, we tested whether social identity complexity (the extent to which individuals view their ingroups as differentiated rather than overlapping) was associated with intergroup bias in spontaneous stereotype valence. Consistent with classic intergroup patterns, participants generated more positive stereotypes for targets who shared more of their social group memberships. Social identity complexity moderated this bias by reducing the positivity of ingroup stereotypes rather than by enhancing evaluations of outgroup targets. To illuminate this process, we examined two potential mechanisms: ingroup attachment and perceived diagnosticity of social categories. Results aligned with an indirect effect through lower ingroup attachment, but not through perceived diagnosticity. These findings show that perceivers’ representations of their own social identities meaningfully shape how they spontaneously stereotype others, primarily by reducing ingroup favoritism.

articles.title: Neurodesign-plus: design optimization for constrained event-level fMRI paradigms
articles.authors: Atharv Amar Umap; Caroline J Charpentier; Valentin Guigon
articles.abstract: Task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) experiments are implemented by scheduling events of interest. The schedule specifies their order, durations, and intervening intervals. Together with the acquisition and first-level model specifications, these choices determine the design matrices used for analysis and therefore how precisely task-related blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses can be detected or estimated. Constructing an appropriate schedule is therefore a crucial part of task design, requiring trade-offs among statistical efficiency, sequence predictability, and scan duration. Neurodesign searches for efficient schedules by scoring candidates on four optimality criteria and using genetic-algorithm or simulation-based methods to identify high-scoring designs. However, Neurodesign represents each trial as a single stimulus event with global duration and pre-event, post-event, and inter-trial timing parameters. It therefore cannot directly encode trials containing multiple ordered events or intervals whose durations depend on the events they separate. Neurodesign-plus is a maintained fork that extends the optimization framework to support multi-event trials, probabilistic templates, transition-dependent intervals, and fixed event orders and durations. These additions widen the space of schedules that researchers can generate, represent, and score, thereby improving task-fMRI design optimization.

articles.title: Fooled by Frequency—or Enlightened by It?
articles.authors: Daniel Nikitin; Keisuke Fukuda
articles.abstract: Humans tend to prefer a frequently sampled option over an infrequently sampled option even when the latter is more likely to result in a reward (i.e., frequency bias). To investigate the underlying mechanism of this “seemingly irrational” bias, we had participants (psychology undergraduate students) estimate the reward rate and their confidence in the estimate for both options. Across two experiments (N = 173), we found that 1) reward rate estimates were more accurate for frequently sampled options and 2) confidence in estimation accuracy was unaffected by the sampling frequency. Importantly, when frequently sampled options had objectively poor reward rates, participants shifted their preference toward the infrequently sampled option, suggesting that frequent sampling improved their ability to identify the better option. These results suggest that frequency bias reflects a “rational” use of frequently sampled information rather than an irrational distortion of reward-rate estimation or confidence.

articles.title: Angular Discrepancy and Personality Functioning Across Interpersonal Circumplex Surfaces
articles.authors: Kimberly J. Gilbert; Christopher James Hopwood
articles.abstract: Multisurface interpersonal assessment (MSIA) compares interpersonal circumplex (IPC) profiles across surfaces such as problems, sensitivities, values, and efficacies. A core premise of MSIA is that cross-surface discrepancy, the degree to which interpersonal themes align or diverge across these surfaces, carries clinical meaning beyond the elevation of any single surface, yet this assumption has rarely been tested directly. The present study operationalized cross-surface discrepancy as the angular distance between surface peaks and examined its association with personality functioning in 1,101 community adults. Greater discrepancy between problems and efficacies (r = -.47) and problems and values (r = -.37) predicted higher levels of personality functioning and explained incremental variance beyond surface elevations (change in R² = .034 and .044). Follow-up analyses suggested that people whose primary problems involved being too cold had higher personality functioning if they had values and efficacies in non-cold regions of the IPC. Associations between personality functioning and problems-sensitivities discrepancy were mostly explained by shared interpersonal dysfunction, and non-problem pairs showed negligible effects. These findings offer initial evidence that people who tend to have problems being too cold have higher levels of personality functioning to the degree they value and can engage in non-cold interpersonal behaviors.

articles.title: Affective Abstraction and Emotion Differentiation Across Development
articles.authors: Miłka S. Waniak; Chantal A. Valdivia-Moreno; Ajay Satpute; Erik C Nook
articles.abstract: To master a culture’s categorical systems, growing minds must learn both to identify abstract similarities that bind two individual instances into a common category (e.g., recognizing what makes Scooby and Snoopy both “dogs”) and to differentiate instances that belong to different categories (e.g., calling Garfield a “cat” rather than a “dog”). Research has charted how children learn to “lump” and “split” categories in the cognitive literature, but we know much less about how emotion categories develop. Here, we administered laboratory tasks assessing affective abstraction (i.e., the ability to match two images that induce similar affective experiences) and emotion differentiation (i.e., how specifically one categorizes one’s emotions as distinct) to a cross-sectional sample of participants in the USA aged 10-25 (50.62% women). Affective abstraction scores were largely uncorrelated with age, but the ability to match cross-category stimuli of the same valence (e.g., a negative-affect-inducing house and a negative-affect-inducing animal) increased with age. Interestingly, affective abstraction and emotion differentiation scores were positively associated, especially in youth participants. Thus, abstraction and differentiation are not merely opposites of each other (i.e., it’s not the case that people either tend to chronically “lump” emotion categories or chronically “split” emotion categories). Instead, there may be shared cognitive processes that allow individuals to construct emotion categories that are both nuanced and general enough to conform to societal norms, and this covariance is most pronounced in youth. These results shed new light on the development of emotion categorization.

articles.title: AI Overviews Reduce Search Result Engagement & May Influence Attitude Polarization
articles.authors: Saloni Dash; Yiwei Xu; Lei Cai; Sterling Williams-Ceci; Wang Liao; Emma Spiro
articles.abstract: AI-generated overviews (AIOs) increasingly appear at the top of search result pages, making them the first, and potentially only, content users encounter during search. Despite their widespread adoption, their impact on information seeking, processing, and downstream attitudes remains critically underexplored. Across two preregistered experiments (N = 2,797), we randomly assigned participants to view AIOs on one of four contested topics manipulated to be attitude-congruent, attitude-incongruent, or balanced (only Study 2) relative to their prior attitudes. Participants who viewed an AIO, irrespective of content, were significantly less likely to engage with subsequent search results than control (no AIO). Participants perceived attitude-incongruent AIOs as more biased and weaker than attitude-congruent AIOs. Despite this, attitude-incongruent AIOs reduced attitude polarization relative to attitude-congruent AIOs in Study 1, but not in Study 2 (although directionally consistent). Taken together, these findings suggest that AIOs significantly influence information seeking and processing and raise critical concerns for democratic deliberation.

articles.title: How Social Context Shapes Perceived Identity Overlap:  Evidence from Christian Democrats
articles.authors: Trystan Loustau; Liane Young
articles.abstract: Why do some people perceive two social identities as fitting together while others see them as largely distinct? We propose that these perceptions are shaped, in part, by the social environments in which people live. We tested this model using Christian Democrats, whose religious and political identities often violate prevailing partisan stereotypes. Two observational studies (Ns = 505 and 484) showed that local political (Democratic voting margins) and religious (Christian prevalence) contexts predicted perceived support for Christian and Democratic identities. Specifically, living in more Democratic counties was associated with greater perceived support for Democrats and lower perceived support for Christians, whereas living in more Christian counties was generally associated with greater perceived support for Christians and lower perceived support for Democrats. In turn, greater perceived support for either identity was associated with perceiving Christian and Democratic identities as more overlapping. Consistent with this model, a preregistered experiment (N = 769) demonstrated that increasing perceived support for Christians increased perceived overlap between Christian and Democratic identities. Across studies, greater perceived overlap was selectively associated with warmer evaluations of Christian and Republican targets, suggesting that when people perceive their identities as not fitting together, they may reaffirm one identity (e.g., Democrat) by distancing themselves from the competing identity (e.g., Christian) and salient outgroup members (e.g., Republicans). Together, these findings suggest that perceptions of identity overlap are shaped by social environments and identify perceived social support as one mechanism through which social environments influence these perceptions.

articles.title: Increasing Governmental Efficacy Beliefs Drives Support for Congestion Pricing Policy
articles.authors: Danielle Goldwert; Anandita Sabherwal; Madalina Vlasceanu
articles.abstract: Congestion pricing charges drivers a fee to enter high-traffic areas, reducing congestion and travel times while generating revenue for public transit and lowering air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Despite its effectiveness, the policy remains contentious because it imposes immediate, salient personal costs in exchange for benefits that are less tangible, delayed, and distributed across both individuals (e.g., shorter, more reliable trips) and society (e.g., cleaner air, safer streets, and improved public transit). This asymmetry between how costs and benefits are experienced poses a challenge to public support, which is essential for both the adoption and long-term durability of the policy. Across two large-scale experiments conducted in New York State (N = 15,014) and Washington, D.C. (N = 4,030), we tested 24 psychologically informed interventions designed to increase support for congestion pricing. Increasing governmental outcome efficacy beliefs, by emphasizing that the policy enables government to deliver meaningful public benefits, emerged as the most effective strategy, increasing support for congestion pricing by 30%, while also improving perceptions of the policy's effectiveness and fairness. These effects were robust across intervention delivery modes that varied in participant engagement and did not differ by political affiliation. Together, these findings identify policy-specific outcome efficacy as a scalable and politically robust communication strategy for building public support for sustainable transportation policies.

articles.title: Shared Neurobiological and Computational Mechanisms of Psychedelic, Contemplative, and Fasting-Induced Mystical Experience
articles.authors: Alex Jinich-Diamant
articles.abstract: Psychedelics, contemplative practice, and fasting are physiologically unrelated interventions that nevertheless converge, across cultures and centuries, on a common experiential endpoint: the mystical state. Here I propose that this convergence reflects shared disruption of a single computational architecture, the precision-weighted predictive hierarchy, through three mechanistically distinct but functionally equivalent routes. Serotonergic psychedelics sensitize layer 5 pyramidal neurons and disinhibit higher-order thalamic nuclei, relaxing the gain on top-down priors; open-monitoring meditation shifts thalamocortical coupling geometry toward diffuse, matrix-type connectivity, elevating cortical entropy; and caloric restriction attenuates the metabolic machinery sustaining high-level attractor states, destabilizing the default mode network from below. All three routes terminate in a transient near-critical regime characterized by relaxed priors, scale-free cortical dynamics, and expanded degrees of freedom in the brain's generative model, conditions I identify as the neurobiological substrate of mystical experience. Critically, the depth of this state, not its pharmacological or procedural occasion, is the primary predictor of lasting therapeutic benefit, implicating conscious experience itself as the mechanistic agent of change. I further argue that near-critical dynamics may constitute the conditions under which field-theoretic and quantum-coherent contributions to consciousness become empirically detectable. This framework generates testable predictions across molecular, circuit, and phenomenological levels, and positions the neuroscience of mystical states as a tractable frontier for understanding how the brain constructs, maintains, and fundamentally reorganizes its model of reality.

articles.title: Beyond Color: A Constructivist Account of Chromatic Stimuli as Multidimensional Physiological and Psychological Events
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: Color science has spent most of its history explaining one thing: the conscious sensation of hue, saturation, and brightness. Yet beside that success sits a growing list of inconvenient findings. Examples include ambiguous colors (one photograph seen as white-and-gold by some and blue-and-black by others); memory colors (a gray banana that looks faintly yellow); color before form (newly sighted patients who see color before objects); imagined or dreamed colors (chromatic experiences generated without light or eyes); aphantasia (people who cannot summon a color in imagination); synesthesia (a printed letter flooded with color); and large, stable individual differences in the colors people report. These are not marginal curiosities or isolated anomalies. They are the ordinary output of a system that the percept-centered framework leaves out. A chromatic stimulus does not simply produce a color percept; it initiates a broad physiological and psychological event, of which the percept is only one part. That percept is constructed at the moment of seeing by memory, language, attention, affect, and culture, and it shapes them in turn, a reciprocal determinism of percept and event. I develop this framework at three levels, as two nested theories: a new theory of color contained within a constructivist model of the entire chromatic event. The account retains trichromatic and some opponent-process theory rather than replacing them, but extends them by predicting phenomena the traditional framework treats as noise.
