value for compression of these AI-inferred dimensions - regardless of source of inference.

articles.title: Rationally Selected Utility – A New Theory of Riskless Choice
articles.authors: Shreya Sinha; Agnieszka Tymula; Paul Glimcher
articles.abstract: Traditional prescriptive decision theories from Pascal’s Expected Value to Expected Utility have struggled to explain inconsistent human choices, leading to purely descriptive models like prospect theory. This paper introduces a novel approach to understand why these behaviors occur, reconciling these observed irrationalities with a simple rational objective, specifically in the domain of riskless choice when choosing between options with certain outcomes. Here, we propose that the human nervous system, faced with limited cognitive capacity (a finite representational precision for the subjective values of rewards), optimally selects a task-appropriate utility function to either maximize long-run average earnings or to minimize errors when choosing between certain outcomes. We argue that the utility functions psychologists and economists have measured empirically are tools, sculpted by knowledge of the choice environment's probabilistic structure and the decision-maker's precision level, for optimally achieving a rational objective. Our results show that almost every experimentally observed utility function can be described as a near-optimal tool for achieving a maximization of objective earnings, a goal abandoned since Bernoulli. We quantify the specific gains that result when a chooser decides to add more cognitive capacity when facing a choice and find that these gains are quite small as long as the utility function is rationally selected. Our research provides a novel framework that offers a testable and foundational explanation for why human and animal decision-makers evolved the puzzling range of utility functions and risk attitudes that have been observed empirically.

articles.title: Hindustani Classical Music and the Cognitive Brain: Revisiting Music Cognition through a Non-Western Lens
articles.authors: Aratrika Patnaik; Vaibhav Tripathi
articles.abstract:
The influence of music on affective and cognitive processes has been widely explored; however,
much of this exploration is limited to Western stimuli and samples, which may lead to a lack of
generalizability in findings and basing models around them. This work introduces Hindustani
Classical Music as an ideal case that raises questions around the cross-cultural validity of these
findings. Hindustani music, with its system of ragas, follows a unique structural pattern that
gives each raga its own emotional identity, and performance is primarily based around
improvisation and ornamentation, hence making it the ideal testcase for making theoretical and
empirical comparisons. It critically reviews empirical evidence across five cognitive domains –
emotions, memory, imagery, embodiment, and predictive processing, concluding with an applied
therapeutic implication as a consequence of these domains. Each domain includes a section
wherein findings from HCM-based studies converge with those of Western studies and then
divulges into findings that are distinct and unique for HCM, such as that of the bhava-rasa
system, the memory-improvisation relationship, internally generated pulse, and culturally-coded
imagery, factors that Western models may not fully be able to explain. The consistent
convergence-divergence reflects that although cognitive processes may be influenced by music
in a general manner, this is true only to a certain extent. Other findings may be more system-
specific and thus reflect that paradigms and models of studying music cognition cannot be
limited to one tradition. The review concludes with future directions for developing paradigms to
study the influence of HCM on cognition in a more systematic and culturally relevant manner.

articles.title: Health Behaviour Pathways to Internalising Symptoms in Adolescence. A Random Intercepts Latent Transition Analysis
articles.authors: Christopher Knowles; Qiqi Cheng; Neil Humphrey
articles.abstract: Adolescence is marked by simultaneous declines in mental health and the everyday health behaviours that support it. Whether the pathway adolescents take through changing constellations of physical activity, diet, and sleep carries information about mental health over and above their current constellation, remains unclear. We used three annual waves of #BeeWell data (N = 42,944; School Years 8 to 10; ages 12–15) collected from two English regions from 2021 to 2025 to estimate a Random Intercept Latent Transition Analysis of physical activity, fruit and vegetable consumption, and sleep. A four-class solution was replicated at each wave, distinguishing Healthy, Low PA with Good Diet, High PA with Poor Diet, and Unhealthy classes, with equivalent classes becoming marginally less healthy over time. Year 10 class predicted concurrent internalising symptoms (Unhealthy vs Healthy d = .18) however, once Year 10 class was accounted for, the pathway by which adolescents arrived there contributed little additional information. Findings from the current study suggest that what adolescents do now matters, but the path they took may not. Health-reinforcing behaviours remain worth pursuing based on the effects of endpoint alone.

articles.title: Recontextualizing Cultural Humility in the Japanese Counseling Context: Development and Validation of the MCHS-J
articles.authors: Yuni Eeh; Miho Tahakashi
articles.abstract:
Although cultural humility has become a central professional orientation in
multicultural counseling, researchers have rarely examined its underlying structure
outside Western contexts. Therefore, using data from 126 Japanese mental health
professionals and graduate students, this study translated, culturally adapted, and
psychometrically evaluated the Japanese version of the Multidimensional Cultural
Humility Scale. Target-rotated exploratory structural equation modeling supported a
revised 4-factor, 11-item structure consisting of Openness, Self-Awareness,
Egolessness, and Self-Reflection and Critique, eliminating one Openness item and the
entire Supportive Interactions dimension. This revised scale showed adequate internal
consistency and a clear, simple structure. Its criterion-related validity was supported as
well: after controlling for socially desirable responding, associations with intercultural
sensitivity and working alliance remained substantial. These findings suggest an item-
and factor-level reorganization of cultural humility within the Japanese counseling
context, rendering cross-cultural adaptation as less a matter of linguistic transfer than of
empirically recontextualizing a psychological construct within local models of the self
and interpersonal relationships.

articles.title: Inclusive Neurodiverse Campuses: A participatory approach to understanding neurodivergent belonging in higher education
articles.authors: Lorna Hamilton; Jamie Williams; Darcy Neilson; Stephanie Petty
articles.abstract: A sense of belonging is linked to people’s engagement, performance and wellbeing in educational and workplace settings. However, previous literature on belonging at university lacks conceptual clarity, often using unidimensional measures that foreground social integration, which may not be valid and transferable to neurodivergent students and employees. Adopting an inclusive definition of neurodivergence, we report a participatory action research project in the context of a university in northern England, with the aim of understanding and promoting belonging on campus. At the first phase, 152 anonymous contributions were received across a multi-media cross-campus installation. Data were analysed using conventional content analysis, which identified key determinants of belonging for neurodivergent people: (1) Meaningful inclusive practice, characterised by flexibility and choice in learning, inclusion by default, validation and being believed; (2) Neurodivergent representation as a shared responsibility, supported by identity spaces and visible acceptance of difference; and (3) Navigating time, space and transition, highlighting the interdependency between space and experience, via constant cost-benefit decision-making. These themes informed a second phase of in-depth interviews with staff and students (n=13), analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings are presented as a Model of Neurodivergent Belonging at University, framed through five questions that people negotiate to actively construct a sense of belonging in their contexts. We conclude that belonging at university for neurodivergent people requires authentic acceptance, rather than assimilation or institutional affiliation. Making small, achievable changes across university systems can cascade into meaningful gains in success and wellbeing for neurodivergent people.

articles.title: The Development of Sensitivity to Automatic Behavior
articles.authors: Ilona Bass; Elizabeth Bonawitz; Tomer David Ullman
articles.abstract: People’s behavior can be roughly categorized into two modes: reflective and thoughtful, or automatic and rote. Past work on Theory of Mind has focused on how children reason about the first category of behavior. But do children also notice when other people are acting in an automatic way? And if so, when might this matter? This paper examined 5- to 10-year-old children’s reasoning about others’ rote behavior, mainly focusing on the consequences of this inference in teaching contexts (N = 660 across four studies, 327 girls; data collected online from U.S.-based children between May 2022 and December 2024). Children’s sensitivity to apparent rote behavior increased with development, with more consistent inferences emerging around age 7. Rote behavior was also associated with worse teaching. These results indicate when and how reasoning about automatic behavior matters to children’s perception of others, and suggest novel extensions to models of Theory of Mind.

articles.title: Aversion to intergroup inequality can be leveraged to promote intergroup cooperation
articles.authors: Filippo Toscano; Martin Götz; Katharina Reher; Jörg Gross
articles.abstract: Tackling global challenges necessitates cooperation beyond group boundaries. This requires groups to reallocate resources from serving only their group members to creating public goods that benefit everyone. Such a transition to intergroup cooperation can be particularly challenging when certain groups benefit more strongly from group cooperation, because these advantaged groups may have little interest in establishing cooperative relationships with other groups. Using interactive experiments and computational modelling, we show how such structural inequality between groups creates systematic barriers to the emergence of intergroup cooperation and how these can be overcome. Specifically, while structural inequality undermines intergroup cooperation, a minority of members of advantaged groups show a concern for intergroup fairness (Study 1, N = 378). These fairness motives can be systematically leveraged through peer enforcement to promote intergroup cooperation (Study 2, N = 360). We show that peer enforcement is used not only to sanction free-riding but also to establish a norm of intergroup cooperation, discouraging exclusive in-group cooperation even among advantaged groups. Our findings challenge the notion that human cooperation is inherently biased towards the in-group. Instead, we provide evidence for an aversion to intergroup inequality that can be harnessed to establish intergroup cooperation even amid structural inequality.

articles.title: The Effects of Online Enactive Education on Secondary School Students
articles.authors: Deborah R. Vivo
articles.abstract: Enactive education is an innovative model based on embodied cognition. This quasi-experimental controlled study with pretest-posttest design investigated the effects of an online enactive school program on students’ learning outcomes, academic self-concept, and physical self-concept. The study was conducted in three secondary schools in the districts of Salerno and Potenza, Italy, during COVID-19 school closures in 2021. Participants were 431 students, 52.4% girls, mean age 14.27 years (SD = 1.01). The study instruments included a school questionnaire and the academic and physical scales of the multidimensional self-concept scale (MSCS). The experimental group received online sessions on mind-body wellbeing, healthy eating, and movement, while controls received non-enactive online classes on the same subjects. Findings indicate that the experimental group, compared to controls, showed higher levels of all the variables considered. Implications include that online enactive education should be used at secondary school level to promote desirable educational and psychological outcomes.

articles.title: The cognitive foundations of food moralization
articles.authors: Isobel Azani Heck; Charlotte Sophia Borgers; Tamar Kushnir
articles.abstract: By adulthood, we attach moral valence to food—labeling some foods as “good,” others as “bad,” and judging ourselves and others based on the foods we choose. Here, we examined young children’s beliefs about which foods are permissible to eat and whether these conceptions vary across early childhood––shifting patterns of normative alignment that may reflect early internalization of societal beliefs about food and lay a cognitive foundation for food moralization. We presented 4- to 6-year-old children with 12 foods (four healthy, four unhealthy, four of mixed-health status; based on adult health ratings) and asked children to categorize each as “healthy” or “not healthy” (Health); “liked” or “not liked” (Desirability); and “OK” or “not OK” (Permissibility). Although children’s Desirability categorizations were similar across ages (with unhealthy foods categorized as “liked” most often), older (vs. younger) children’s Health and Permissibility categorizations were more closely aligned with each other and with adult health judgments. Moreover, whereas younger children positively associated Permissibility with Desirability, older children did not. In contrast, a positive association between Permissibility and Health was stronger among older children. Parents’ food-related behaviors further predicted differences in how children conceptualized Permissibility. Together, these findings reveal differences across early childhood in beliefs regarding what is permissible to eat––shifting patterns that may lay a foundation on which food moralization is built. The work paves the way for continued research on the emergence and consequences of food moralization and for efforts to teach about health in ways that support healthy relationships with food.

articles.title: Individual differences in silent and filled pause production in spontaneous speech: Speaker-level and speech-level factors
articles.authors: Kyla McConnell; Franziska Margarete Schulz; antje meyer; Ruth Corps
articles.abstract: Speech is rarely completely fluent, and disfluencies, such as silent and filled pauses, can arise from difficulties in speech planning. Yet it remains unclear whether pause rates are driven by characteristics of the speaker, characteristics of the utterance, or interactions between the two. We analysed one-minute recordings of spontaneous speech from 112 participants who answered three open-ended questions in a test session and again in a re-test session after four weeks (Hintz et al., 2020a). Results showed that pause rates exhibited test–retest reliability and were consistent across elicitation questions. However, mixed-effects models showed that pause rates were not explained solely by the speaker-level factors of short-term memory, processing speed, or linguistic experience. Across analyses, speech-level factors, particularly word frequency, were the most consistent predictors of both silent and filled pauses. Importantly, the effect of word frequency was moderated by processing speed: speakers with slower processing speed showed stronger frequency effects, resulting in a higher predicted rate of filled pauses for utterances with low frequency words. Together, these findings suggest that while speech fluency is a stable characteristic of individual speakers, moment-to-moment disfluencies emerge from dynamic interactions between speakers' cognitive capacities and the planning demands of particular utterances.

articles.title: Descriptions of phenomenal versus intentional mental states are differentially associated with gaze direction
articles.authors: Mohit Mukherji; Moira Rose Dillon
articles.abstract: Across cultures, humans reason about others’ mental states as being either phenomenal, reflecting shareable experiences, or intentional, reflecting agentive goals. Might our dissociated judgments of others’ mental states be linked to dissociated judgments of others’ gaze direction, one of our earliest social cues from infancy? We presented adults (N = 600) and 6- to 8-year-old children (N = 200) with direct, definitional descriptions as well as descriptions of example phenomenal or intentional mental states and asked them to choose whether a face with averted or straight-ahead gaze better matched the character in each description. Adults and older children chose the averted-gaze face for the direct phenomenality description but the straight-ahead-gaze face for the direct intentionality description. Adults showed the same pattern of responses for the indirect, example descriptions, but children chose the straight-ahead-gaze face for both types of indirect descriptions. Descriptions of either phenomenal or intentional mental states might be intuitively associated with straight-ahead gaze, perhaps originating in infants’ understanding of straight-ahead gaze as communicating either mutual social engagement or general visible accessibility for goal-directed action. The association between phenomenality descriptions and averted gaze may, by contrast, arise only after learning that certain phenomenal contexts involve inner experiences with averted gaze (e.g., someone is looking at a particular emotion-evoking stimulus or looking “into their own mind”). If, in adulthood, our social concepts have indeed been built on prelinguistic intuitions that can be evoked by language, then these intuitions may continue to affect our mature, linguistically driven social reasoning.

articles.title: Professionals of trust: Intermediaries concentrate exchanges, creating incentives for reliability
articles.authors: Julien Lie-Panis; Jean-Baptiste André; Helena Miton
articles.abstract: Trade is most profitable when partners are distant, but also most fragile, because distance makes it harder to trust that others will keep their side of the bargain. When exchange stretches beyond local ties, societies often rely on intermediaries—merchants, brokers, auctioneers, and other professionals who stand between buyers and sellers. At first glance this solution is paradoxical: why would inserting a third party create trust? Intermediation adds another link in the chain—another stranger who can misrepresent quality, divert goods, or renege on payment. We propose that intermediation creates trust by concentrating exchanges onto fewer reputations, raising the cost of any single failure and strengthening incentives for reliable conduct. We formalize this idea in a model of reputation-based cooperation, involving buyers, suppliers, and intermediaries. The model yields two trade regimes: direct buyer–supplier exchange, where suppliers build reputations with buyers, and intermediated exchange, where intermediaries broker transactions and build reputations with buyers instead. Comparing the two, we show that intermediation expands the scope of trade—and that this extension can arise purely from scarcity: as intermediaries become fewer, each handles more transactions, raising the reputational cost of unreliable trade. Intermediaries, in this view, are professionals of trust: they can be relied on because they have the most to lose.

articles.title: From Human to AI: Cognitive Mechanisms Underlying the Associations between Insecure Interpersonal Attachment Styles and Human-AI Emotional Engagement
articles.authors: Chuqi Chen; Huiguang Ren; Junsheng Liu; Fanlong Wang; Shijia Ji; Fangfang Tian
articles.abstract: Attachment styles have long been shown to shape how individuals form and maintain interpersonal relationships. Extending this perspective to human-AI interaction, the present study examined whether and how individuals’ interpersonal attachment styles were linked to their human-AI emotion-related behaviors and attachment. We further tested whether this process was mediated by cognitive perceptions related to AI’s emotional capacity (i.e., perceived uniqueness of AI) and moderated by individuals’ cognitive disposition to view non-living entities as human-like (i.e., dispositional anthropomorphism). Participants were a regionally representative sample of 1,406 undergraduate students (Mage = 18.98 years, SD = 1.25; 40% male) recruited from 26 universities in Shanghai, China, using a stratified random sampling procedure. Participants reported on their interpersonal attachment styles, perceived uniqueness of AI, anthropomorphism, and two indicators of emotional engagement with AI: personal disclosure and emotional attachment. Results showed that both interpersonal attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance were positively associated with perceived uniqueness of AI, which was in turn associated with greater personal disclosure and stronger emotional attachment to AI. Anthropomorphism further moderated the association between perceived uniqueness of AI and emotional engagement, such that these associations were stronger among individuals with higher levels of anthropomorphism. Similarly, moderated mediation analyses indicated that the indirect effects of interpersonal attachment orientations on emotional engagement with AI through perceived uniqueness of AI were amplified at higher levels of anthropomorphism. Overall, the findings suggest that human-AI emotional engagement may be shaped by both individuals’ human-human attachment-related orientations and their psychological construal of AI as a human-like, relationally meaningful interaction partner.

articles.title: Robust circular cluster-based statistics for respiration-brain coupling
articles.authors: Teresa Berther; Elio Balestrieri; Martina Saltafossi; Laura Bock Paulsen; Lau Møller Andersen; Daniel Kluger
articles.abstract: The rapidly developing research field of brain-body neuroscience faces methodological challenges, as analysts continue to develop new analysis strategies for robust statistics in the absence of established best practices. This quest for robust statistics is further complicated by the (naturally) circular data involved in the study of phase-locked effects, e.g. in respiration-brain coupling. Circularity of respiratory data particularly affects the problem of multiple comparisons in phase-related inferential statistics. In this tutorial, we propose a robust pipeline for respiration-related analyses based on a circular extension of cluster-based permutation testing we developed. We highlight and offer guidance on critical parameters in the analysis, systematically compare various approaches being used in the field today, and provide open-access software code for flexible use and future development of our proposed pipeline.

articles.title: Mapping Mechanistic Interactions Between Layers of Presence and the Human Affectome
articles.authors: Oliver Singleton
articles.abstract: The sense of presence - the feeling of 'being there' in an environment - is a foundational concept in consciousness research, yet its relationship to human affect remains theoretically underdeveloped. Although presence and emotion are known to interact, prior accounts have treated this relationship as either unidirectional or have failed to specify which aspects of affect interact with which layers of presence. The present paper addresses this gap by proposing a model that maps mechanistic interactions between the layers of presence, as conceptualised by Riva et al. (2004), and the components of the human affectome, as taxonomised by Schiller et al. (2024). This paper argues that the affective features valence and arousal share bidirectional relationships with core presence, such that moment-to-moment affective quality both shapes and is shaped by the organism's felt engagement with the immediate environment. We further argue that the global affective concerns of trajectory and optimisation share bidirectional relationships with extended presence, such that long-timescale affective states both disrupt and are regulated by the organism's autobiographical, trans-temporal self. The hierarchy of affective concern, termed distance, is proposed to influence core presence unidirectionally, with more immediate concerns having greater impact than distal ones. These relationships are defended using a combination of empirical evidence from virtual reality research and convergent clinical observations from depersonalisation-derealisation disorder, depression, dementia and anosognosia. The model generates four testable hypotheses for future empirical investigation and offers a more granular and mechanistically precise account of the presence-affect relationship than has previously been proposed.

articles.title: Effects of the distribution of acoustic cues on infants' perception of sibilants
articles.authors: Alejandrina Cristia; Grant L. McGuire; Amanda Seidl; Alexander L. Francis; Alex Eguiluz
articles.abstract: A current theoretical view proposes that infants converge on the speech categories of their native language by attending to frequency distributions that occur in the acoustic input. To date, the only empirical support for this statistical learning hypothesis comes from studies where a single, salient dimension was manipulated. Additional evidence is sought here, by introducing a less salient pair of categories supported by multiple cues. We exposed English-learning infants to a multi-cue bidimensional grid between retroflex and alveolopalatal sibilants in prevocalic position. This contrast is substantially more difficult according to previous cross-linguistic and perceptual research, and its perception is driven by cues in both the consonantal and the following vowel portions. Infants heard one of two distributions (flat, or with two peaks), and were tested with sounds varying along only one dimension. Infants’ responses differed depending on the familiarization distribution, and their performance was equally good for the vocalic and the frication dimension, lending some support to the statistical hypothesis even in this harder learning situation. However, learning was restricted to the retroflex category, and a control experiment showed that lack of learning for the alveolopalatal category was not due to the presence of a competing category. Thus, these results contribute fundamental evidence on the extent and limitations of the statistical hypothesis as an explanation for infants’ perceptual tuning.

articles.title: The kaleidoscope of distress: elevated negative emodiversity across objective and idiographic cognitive tasks is associated with worse mental health in adolescence
articles.authors: Alice Roe; Tim Dalgleish
articles.abstract:
Background
Greater complexity in one’s emotional experience is thought to support mental health, including increased diversity in experienced emotions (emodiversity). However, findings linking emodiversity to psychological wellbeing in adults have been mixed, and little is known about its role during adolescence. We examined whether emodiversity across two different emotional contexts – related to self-referential material and to emotional responses to everyday visual scenes – was associated with mental ill-health symptomatology in a community sample of adolescents. 
Methods
Three-hundred-and-thirty-five adolescents (Mage = 17.1, SD = 0.6, 81.8% female, 71.3% White British) completed two task-based measures of emotional experience, related to the self-concept and standardised visual stimuli, alongside self-report measures of depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress symptoms, and emotion regulation.  
Results
Greater negative emodiversity across both tasks was associated with elevated depression and anxiety symptoms, while post-traumatic stress symptoms were associated with greater negative emodiversity for the self-concept only. Lower positive emodiversity for the self-concept was also associated with poorer mental health. There was a small, positive association between the two measures of emodiversity. Negative emodiversity for the self-concept was associated with greater use of maladaptive emotion regulation strategies.
Conclusions
Findings suggest that elevated negative emodiversity may represent a transdiagnostic marker of mental ill-health symptomatology in adolescence and highlights the importance of examining different emotional contexts to further elucidate the relationship between emotional complexity and mental health.

articles.title: Memory Benefits for Schematically Incongruent Sequences Depend on the Type of Violation
articles.authors: Adam James Curtis; Darcy Denneen; Maria Wimber; Aidan J Horner
articles.abstract: Schemas, knowledge structures that represent regularities across episodes, can enhance memory for events that are either congruent or incongruent with their content. Across four experiments including 193 university students, we investigated whether these schema effects emerge when chronology forms a core aspect of a schema’s content, enabling temporal predictions of future events. After pre-training on schematically defined four-item sequences, participants studied novel sequences that either affirmed, violated, or were unrelated to these schemas. Memory benefits were observed for both schematically congruent and incongruent sequences relative to sequences that were schema-unrelated. Critically, incongruent memory benefits only emerged for violations of content, and not for violations of temporal order, despite behavioural evidence of prediction error at encoding for both violation types. Our findings show that schema effects depend on the type of schematic violation and that incongruent benefits are not the inevitable consequence of prediction error at encoding.

articles.title: How participants confound experiments by generating desired experiences
articles.authors: Peter Lush; Zoltan Dienes; Anil Seth; Ryan Bradley Scott
articles.abstract: Since 18th century experiments demonstrated that the effects of mesmerism arose from belief rather than magnetic fluid, there has been evidence that situational cues can drive change in experience. Across four studies (total N = 2,042), we investigated the degree to which experiences in psychological experiments may arise from participants controlling their experience to satisfy their goals, i.e., phenomenological control. Trait phenomenological control predicts some experimental measures of changes in experience when demand characteristics are not controlled. Here, we investigated the reach of phenomenological control as a demand effect by contrasting relationships between Phenomenological Control Scale scores (PCS) and effects presumed to either be highly sensitive to beliefs (visually evoked auditory response or vEAR; tingling in the scalp or ASMR) or less sensitive to beliefs (Müller Lyer and vertical-horizontal illusions). Phenomenological control accounted for much of the effect for the posited belief-sensitive effects but not for the classic visual illusions (Study 1). This pattern of results remained after controlling for context effects (Study 2) and measurement differences across procedures (Study 3). Finally, Study 4 presents causal evidence that vEAR and ASMR can be modulated by high PCS participants in response to demand characteristics delivered by direct suggestion. When an effect is substantially predicted by trait phenomenological control and can be caused by phenomenological control following demand characteristics, this domain-general mechanism should be ruled out before appealing to domain-specific explanations. This presents a previously unrecognised threat to validity in psychology experiments analogous to that of placebo effects in medicine.

articles.title: Suicide in the community and mental healthcare usage: A nationwide register-based study in the Netherlands
articles.authors: Milan Zarchev; Philip Michielsen; Richard Vijverberg; Marco Helbich
articles.abstract:
Background – suicide bereavement can have profound effects on mental health. It is unclear, however, how suicide in ones community is related to mental health, and whether specific communities, such as socially fragmented or economically deprived one, are affected differently.

Methods – the current register-based study used an longitudinal cohort design (n=702,589) utilizing Dutch national registry data. Communities were identified using address registers to obtain postcode data. Community suicide exposure obtained from death registers was based on number of suicides in postcode during the follow up period. Mental healthcare usage was obtained from basic and specialized mental healthcare registers. We adjusted all association for socioeconomic neighborhood charactersitics. As moderators, we investigated community social fragmentation, proportion of non-Dutch residents, residential density and proportion of low income households.

Results – more community suicide was associated with lower mental healthcare usage (log hazard ratio = -0.37 [95%CI = -0.37, -0.37]). A dose-response like relationship was observed for communities with higher categories of suicide rates and less mental healthcare usage. Socially fragmented communities and those with more migrant residents were least likely to use mental healthcare after high community suicide rates.

Conclusions – communities which experience high suicide rates, especially socially fragmentted and migrant ones, could potentially benefit from more mental healthcare usage to prevent further suicides.

articles.title: The Standardized Open-source Mindfulness Architecture (SOMA): A Modular, Equity-Engineered Stimulus Library for Mechanistic Mindfulness Research
articles.authors: Alessandro Sparacio; Ivan Ropovik; Jonathan Nicholas Davies; Erin Lee; Ted Meissner; Christoph Spiessens; Alina Rodriguez; Johan Gunnar Eriksson
articles.abstract: Mindfulness research faces two recurring methodological problems: near-universal reliance on weak control conditions that cannot isolate specific mechanisms from expectancy effects, and systematic exclusion of low-socioeconomic status (SES) populations through design assumptions that presuppose high literacy, quiet private spaces, and contemplative familiarity. We present the Standardized Open-source Mindfulness Architecture (SOMA), a modular stimulus library designed to address both challenges. SOMA comprises 88 audio/script assets: 32 pre-specified Mindfulness–Active Control session pairs across 16 practice modules, written at Grade 5–6 reading level and designed for noisy, shared environments. A pre-registered validation randomised controlled trial (RCT; N = 360; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07556744) provides proof-of-concept. The data supported the predicted double dissociation (Condition × Measure: F(1, 358) = 185.95, p = 2.2 × 10−34, BF10 ≈ 9.5 × 1063) and experiential equity across SES strata (Hedges' g = −0.07; TOST-confirmed within ±0.40), yet a small credibility gap remained, favouring the Mindfulness condition.

articles.title: Development and Validation of a Multilevel Deep-Learning Framework for Individualized Prediction in Clustered Data
articles.authors: Ningzhe Zhu; Ramona Schoedel; Larissa Sust; Markus Bühner; Yannik Terhorst
articles.abstract: Clustered data are common in psychological studies that collect repeated observations from individuals, classrooms, clinics, or other naturally occurring units. Such data offer rich opportunities for predicting psychological outcomes, but they also pose substantial analytic challenges. Predictors are usually high-dimensional, and the relations between independent and dependent within-level variables may vary across between-level clusters. Traditional statistical models are often restrictive under these conditions, whereas many supervised machine-learning models assume common predictive relations across clusters. To address these limitations, we developed a multilevel deep-learning framework for clustered data. The framework separates stable between-cluster differences from within-cluster deviations while allowing between-level variables to shape how within-level data is processed. It includes three components: (a) a baseline network that predicts each cluster’s typical outcome level from between-level variables, (b) a deviation network that predicts within-level deviations from that baseline using within-level variables, and (c) a slope network that maps between-level variables onto individualized slope vectors that gate within-level variables. We validated the framework using a digital-sensing and experience-sampling dataset and compared its performance against previous state-of-the-art models. The validation sample comprised 483 participants (219 female; Mage = 42.98 years, SD = 12.84), contributing a total of 6,737 days of data. Predictors included 560 daily smartphone-sensing (within-level) variables and 37 person-level (between-level) variables, and the outcome was daily affect. The proposed framework outperformed existing models and provided multiple layers of interpretive opportunities. The framework offers an innovative approach for combining between-level and within-level data in personalized psychological prediction models.

articles.title: Dynamic effects of multiround positive and negative feedback from robots and humans on trust and collaboration
articles.authors: Hongzhou Xuan; Jiaying Zhu; QianenLai; Guibing He
articles.abstract: Human–robot collaboration is gradually emerging as a new mode of work in intelligent organizations. Trust serves as the foundation for cooperation among team members, and it is established and dynamically evolves through interaction. Therefore, it is particularly important to understand how human–robot interaction influences trust and how this process differs from interpersonal interaction. Through one pilot experiment and two formal experiments, the present study examined, from a dynamic perspective, the effects of multi-round feedback from robot versus human sources on the evolution of trust and cooperation. The pilot experiment was conducted to select appropriate positive and negative feedback statements. In the formal experiments, participants collaborated with either a robot or a human teammate to complete five rounds of an investment decision-making task, during which they evaluated each other between rounds. Participants received four rounds of negative feedback from either a robot or a human teammate in Experiment 1, and four rounds of positive feedback in Experiment 2. The results showed that, in the context of multi-round negative feedback, trust and cooperation exhibited a clearer source-dependent pattern. Specifically, under robot-generated negative feedback, trust and cooperation were more likely to follow a “lagged-cumulative” evolutionary pattern, characterized by delayed responses and cumulative effects. In contrast, under human-generated negative feedback, trust and cooperation were more likely to follow an “immediate-responsive” evolutionary pattern, characterized by higher sensitivity and stronger adaptability. However, in the context of multi-round positive feedback, no significant differences were found in the dynamic effects of different feedback sources on trust and cooperation. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding the differentiated evolution of human–robot trust and interpersonal trust from a dynamic perspective, and offers practical implications for the design of feedback strategies in hybrid teams.

articles.title: Sensory hyper-sensitivity associates with poor infant sleep and different parental sleep practices, in a UK cohort
articles.authors: Teodora; Hope Fincham; Anna De Laet; Rachael Bedford
articles.abstract: Sleep difficulties (e.g., increased sleep onset latency and more frequent night awakenings) are common in early development and are associated with increased parental stress. Sleep difficulties have been linked to sensory hypersensitivity in typically developing infants and infants with family history of autism. In the current study, we investigate whether infant sensory sensitivity is associated with the strategies parents employ when settling infants to sleep. Strategies encouraging autonomy, rather than those involving active physical comforting, have previously been shown to lead to better sleep. We report findings from a cross-sectional UK sample of 245 infants aged 6 to 13 months, from which we collected online parent-report measures of infant sleep and sensory sensitivity (ITSP). We replicate previous findings showing that poorer sleep is correlated with higher infant sensory sensitivity. We then show an association between higher infant sensory sensitivity and more frequent use of all settling strategies, as well as a higher number of different strategies used. A strong correlation between infant and maternal sensory sensitivity precluded testing whether parental settling strategies are driven by infant or parental sensory sensitivity. The current findings emphasise the need to integrate information about intrinsic (e.g. infant sensitivity) and social environment factors (e.g. parental sensitivity, settling strategies) to understand infant sleep.

articles.title: People make inferences from policy decisions regarding default options:  Replication and extension of McKenzie et al. (2006)
articles.authors: Xiaoru Teng; Ka Wai LAU; Tsz King Ng; Chan Ka Po; Yeung Wing; Siu Kit Yeung; Gilad Feldman
articles.abstract: Default effect refers to the phenomenon that people tend to choose the default option in a choice-set. McKenzie et al. (2006) showed that one mechanism for the effect is that defaults are perceived as an implicit endorsement and a recommended option by the policy makers that set the defaults. In a pre-registered experiment with a Prolific online sample from the United States (N = 602), we conducted replications and extensions of Studies 1, 2, and 3 from McKenzie et al. (2006). Across the nine target-article tests, the adjusted Cramer's V effects ranged from .24 to .86 with corresponding replication estimates ranging from .41 to .80. We concluded a successful replication of all three studies, with support for their findings showing that: 1) people who report willingness to be organ donors, and people who think others ought to be donors, are more likely to select organ donation as the policy default, and that in turn: 2) people make inferences from policymaker’s set defaults (Study 2: organ donations; Study 3: retirement plans) regarding the policymakers’ own preferences regarding enrollment, and their views regarding whether others should enroll. In our extension we added a control condition with no defaults, finding that 1) people still make inferences about choice architects’ attitudes, even when defaults were not set, and 2) that setting defaults to not act (not enroll) is perceived as closer to no defaults than setting defaults to act (to enroll). Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/E5K4J.

articles.title: From Construct Definitions to Narrative Response Models: The Case of Self-Efficacy
articles.authors: Rik Crutzen; Gjalt - Jorn Peters
articles.abstract: Psychology faces crises of theory and measurement, where poorly specified constructs hinder the validity of measurement instruments. This article turns prior pleas to transparently explicate comprehensive construct definitions and accompanying measurement instructions into practice, using self-efficacy as an exemplary case. Drawing primarily on Bandura’s conceptualization, we explicate the key elements distinguishing self-efficacy from related constructs and examine implications for measurement. More importantly, this is the first time to introduce Narrative Response Models (NRMs) as a tool to describe and study how hypothesized processes that need to occur allow inferences about a psychological construct from the registered responses to an item used to assess that construct (in this case self-efficacy). Without this, there is no reason to assume the responses can tell anything about the construct: the item is invalid. Because NRMs as a tool were developed to justify confidence in the validity of an item, they explicate many underlying assumptions that warrant further investigation. In the case of self-efficacy, for example, the retrieval of gist traces and the simulation of what it takes to engage in the behaviour of interest. As such, NRMs provide scaffolding for the systematic study of a measurement instrument’s validity.

articles.title: An Initial Integration of Constructs that Account for Moral Actions: Moral Foundations, Values and Character Strengths
articles.authors: Richard A. Inman; Uwe Wolfradt; Pedro Joaquim Cardoso Costa; Paulo Alexandre Soares Moreira; René Proyer; Paul H. P. Hanel
articles.abstract: Morality has been described as a psychological system comprising sets of values, practices, institutions, and psychological mechanisms that work together to support moral/socially positive behavior. Nonetheless, there have been relatively few efforts to integrate these diverse constructs. We address this limitation using data from two samples who completed measures of moral foundations (Moral Foundations Theory), values (Schwartz Value Theory), and character strengths (VIA Framework). First, we used principal components analysis to summarize the complex patterns of association among these variables. We then tested whether the extracted components overlapped with normal and maladaptive personality trait domains (HEXACO and DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders). Finally, we tested incremental validity of the three frameworks. In both samples, variance among variables was explained by four components that were suggestive of different “psychological systems” (networks of associated constructs) that may be linked to individual differences in moral action: Universal caring, preservation, self-control, and self-expansion. Further analyses suggested these emergent components are not reducible to single personality domains, each sharing variance with multiple domains. Finally, incremental validity analyses suggested that moral foundations, basic values, and VIA character strengths are complementary rather than redundant constructs, each explaining unique variance in criterion variables (empathy and moral identity).

articles.title: Complementary Indicators of Knowledge Purporting and Their Validity
articles.authors: Benjamin Goecke; Catherine Schittenhelm; Oliver Wilhelm
articles.abstract: Overclaiming (OC)—the tendency to claim knowledge one does not possess—is predominantly assessed through self-report Overclaiming Questionnaires (OCQs). However, exclusive reliance on OCQs raises concerns about mono-method bias, limiting our understanding of knowledge purporting as a broader psychological disposition. To reduce this bias, we investigated two additional indicators of knowledge purporting and examined their convergent validity with traditional OCQs. In our study (N = 297), one of the new measures scored responses on fictional questions and the other captured discrepancies between self-rated knowledge and actual knowledge. Using latent variable analyses, we found modest convergent relations between the three indicators of knowledge purporting. Apart from these substantial levels of method-specific variance, we found differential relations with covariates, thereby challenging the validity and utility of any specific task class, including the predominantly used OCQs. We recommend that knowledge purporting measures must not be equated with the broader concept of knowledge purporting. While this study suggests that the concept of knowledge purporting may have some generality, it also shows that the methods used to investigate it matter more than they should. Future studies should consider the relationship between multivariate measures of knowledge purporting and further discrepancies between self-reports of knowledge and actual performance.

articles.title: The ‘how’ of mental health recovery: Developing a model of internal and external recovery processes using critical realist thematic analysis of first-person online narratives
articles.authors: Quinn William Harper; Amy Mowle; Warren mansell
articles.abstract: Extant mental health recovery frameworks offer valuable thematic summaries, however are ill-equipped to explain how recovery occurs. Their descriptive, individualistic focus fails to account for systemic inequalities or ground new interventions. This study sought to develop an explanatory, general-purpose model of personal recovery by specifying relationships across recovery experiences, the actions leading to them, and the contextual factors these processes depend on. We conducted a tailored form of critical realist thematic analysis on a clinically and demographically diverse sample of 37 mental health recovery narratives from 28 authors within Recovery Diaries: an international online collection of recovery stories. This led to the REACHES model: Recovery Experiences, Actions, and Contexts as a Holistic Explanatory System. REACHES delineates three recovery phases, with each nesting two dialectically opposed recovery processes: individuation involves space and direction; engagement operates via interest and connection; and realisation encompasses perspective and contribution. Each process comprises a recovery action and its resulting recovery experience, and each phase also specifies contextual mechanisms that enable its occurrence. This structure integrates an individual’s complex context (including cultural, social, biological, and structural factors), how they can progress their recovery, and how they may feel as a result into a singular dynamic, explanatory framework. Consequently, REACHES provides versatile avenues for improving mental health outcomes across individual, service-delivery, and policy levels, while holding potential to democratise knowledge across clinicians, peers, and laypeople on how to facilitate recovery. Further research should triangulate and extend REACHES using other samples, data formats, and analytic methods.

articles.title: Beyond Creativity Scores: Changes in Teachers’ Semantic Networks after SCIP Training
articles.authors: Edith Haim; Kurt Haim; Wolfgang Aschauer; Giulio Rossetti; Massimo Stella
articles.abstract: Teacher creativity plays a central role in fostering creative learning environments. However, most evaluations of creativity training focus on performance outcomes and self-report measures rather than changes in underlying cognitive organisation. We investigated whether an eight-month certified teacher-training course based on the Scientific Creativity in Practice (SCIP) framework was associated with changes in Austrian secondary teachers’ creative performance, semantic organisation, and professional mindsets. Seventeen teachers completed pre- and post-training assessments, including the Alternative Uses Task, Verbal Fluency,Word-Sentence-Construction, Behavioural Forma Mentis associations with valence ratings, and written reflections. We assessed originality in the AUT with two independent AI-based systems. Semantic and affective changes were modelled through cognitive networks, mindset streams, and measures of emotional framing. At POST, teachers had higher AUT originality scores and generated largely different concepts than at PRE. They produced broader conceptual repertoires and larger semantic networks, although other structural changes differed across tasks. Affective changes were more modest. Positive valence predominated at both measurement points and became slightly more common, while negative valence declined. Separate PRE and POST mindset streams showed substantial pathway turnover but remained predominantly positive. These findings suggest that creativity training may support changes in how teachers organise and connect professional knowledge, and does not only impact how creatively they perform. Furthermore, our findings show that cognitive network analyses can complement traditional creativity assessments by revealing changes in semantic organisation and professional mindsets that remain invisible in performance scores alone.

articles.title: The Effect of Crime Type and Knowledge about Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC) on the Judgement of Defendants with ASC
articles.authors: Lynn Weiher; Rosa Vermeulen; Hannah Wessels; Steven James Watson
articles.abstract:
Research indicates autistic defendants are treated more leniently than non-autistic defendants. However, it is unclear whether this is caused by positive perceptions of autistic people, or because autism is a relevant mitigating factor. Across two studies we tested how mock jurors evaluated autistic defendants in autism relevant and irrelevant criminal cases to better understand when and why autistic defendants receive leniency. Further, we provided some of the participants with educational information about ASD allowing these participants to recognise autism as a relevant mitigation for criminal cases for which autistic traits can be a risk factor (assault and stalking cases, but not burglary cases).
Defendants with ASD only received lower sentences when autism was a relevant mitigation (assault and stalking), but not when autism was irrelevant (burglary). Thus, participants did not simply give preferential treatment to autistic defendants, but considered how ASD was related to the offense. However, providing information about autism weakened these effects, indicating educating people about autism may not always benefit autistic defendants.
Our study highlights the importance of nuanced messaging about autism. While explaining how autistic characteristics can explain criminal behaviour may reduce perceptions of criminal responsibility, it may also imply greater dangerousness or risk of reoffending.

articles.title: Shortening affect scales for ambulatory assessment: A comparison of different IRT-based approaches
articles.authors: Gudrun Eisele; Esther Ulitzsch; Milla Pihlajamäki; Inez Myin-Germeys; Jindra Bakker; Olivia J Kirtley; Aleksandra Monika Lachowicz; Wim Van Den Noortgate; Stefan Schneider
articles.abstract: Researchers often seek to measure affective experiences in daily life. Consequently, measures of positive and negative affect frequently take up large parts of ambulatory questionnaires. Optimizing questionnaire content and length is crucial in intensive ambulatory studies. In the current study, we developed and tested approaches to shortening ambulatory affect questionnaires. Specifically, we sought to build a preliminary item bank of 14 positive and 20 negative affect items calibrated with a graded response model using data from 14 individual ambulatory assessment studies (N = 3,818). We then compared different IRT-based strategies for shortening affect questionnaires to 2-4 items in simulation studies. Results indicate that computerized adaptive testing, but also simpler, (semi-) static item selection strategies achieve higher precision with the same number of items compared to random selection. We give concrete recommendations and highlight encountered issues and avenues for further refinement of the item bank.

articles.title: The Prospects and Challenges of Measuring a Person’s Overall Moral Goodness
articles.authors: Jessie Sun; Eric Schwitzgebel
articles.abstract: This paper integrates psychological and philosophical theory and research to explain what it would take to measure a person’s general morality (i.e., their overall moral goodness). Conceptually, to measure general morality, there must be general moral facts about people’s overall morality; the measure must correctly identify and weigh those facts; and the measure must apply clearly and consistently across people, groups, and time. We argue that it would be difficult to operationalize morality in a way that satisfies these requirements. Self-report, informant report, behavioral, and biological measurement approaches also have substantial methodological limitations. These conceptual and methodological challenges limit the validity of measures of general morality more than they do for most other psychological traits. This exercise also yields general lessons about the challenges that also confront the design of narrower, less ambitious morality measures (e.g., of specific moral virtues). Some—but not all—of these challenges can be mitigated when the measurement aims are more modest. It is therefore important to be transparent and intellectually humble about what we can and cannot conclude based on various moral assessments. Finally, we outline recommendations and future directions for psychological and philosophical inquiry into the development and use of morality measures.

articles.title: Social Network Centrality and Emotional Dynamics in Classroom Learning: A Multilevel Approach
articles.authors: Alla Hemi; Adar Ben-Eliyahu; Martin Daumiller
articles.abstract:
Background: Students' emotions are shaped both by the structure of their peer relationships and by the affective context of the classroom. Two features of a student's position in the classroom network may matter: being sought out by peers (in-degree centrality), indexing social acceptance, and reaching out to many peers (out-degree centrality), indexing the breadth of active peer engagement. Classroom emotional climate, the aggregated activated affect of the class, may further shape these associations. Yet few studies have examined how a student's network position and the surrounding climate jointly relate to emotional experience.
Aims: We examined how in-degree and out-degree centrality relate to students' emotions across four dimensions (positive and negative, activated and deactivated) and whether classroom emotional climate (aggregated positive or negative activated affect) moderates these relationships.
Sample: Data were collected from 1,284 high school students (50.5% female, Mage = 16.26, SD = 0.88) nested within 56 classrooms.
Methods: We used multilevel structural equation modelling.
Results: Higher out-degree centrality was associated with lower positive activated and lower positive deactivated affect. Higher in-degree centrality was associated with higher positive deactivated affect and with lower negative activated and lower negative deactivated affect. Classroom emotional climate moderated several of these associations: a positive climate attenuated the negative association between out-degree centrality and positive affect, whereas a negative climate weakened the protective association between in-degree centrality and lower negative affect.
Conclusions: Students' network positions were differentially associated with their emotions, and these associations depended on the classroom's emotional climate.

articles.title: Who Is Visible in Autism Research? Demographic Reporting and Representation of Autistic Participants in Australian Autism Studies
articles.authors: Dawn Adams; Megan Walsh; Timea Molnar; Kate Simpson; Simon Bury; Halle Wiblen; Chris Paradisis
articles.abstract: Despite a growing body of autism research, significant gaps remain regarding whose experiences are reported, necessitating a comprehensive assessment of representation across the evidence base. This systematic mapping review examined demographic reporting and representation of autistic participants in Australian autism research published between 2023 and 2025. Searches across 46 academic databases identified 517 Australian autism empirical research articles, of which 467 involved human participants and 272 included demographic data for autistic participants. Demographic reporting of included articles was examined using the PROGRESS-Plus framework alongside priority and intersectional groups identified in Australia's National Autism Strategy. Gender/sex and age were the most frequently reported characteristics, appearing in 89.3% and 74.6% of articles, respectively. In contrast, reporting for First Nations identity, cultural background, socioeconomic status, intellectual disability, communication profiles, sexual orientation+ status, and very high support needs were considerably less common. Eligibility criteria also shaped representation, with many studies requiring a formal autism diagnosis and some excluding participants based on English proficiency, English literacy, intellectual disability, communication profile, or non-speaking status. These findings indicate that many autistic participants remain demographically invisible in autism research, limiting the understanding of whose experiences underpin the evidence base. More consistent demographic reporting, clearer justification of exclusion criteria, and more accessible recruitment and participation methods are needed to support equity, transparency, and policy relevance in autism research. While this study focused on the Australian context, the findings may reflect broader challenges in demographic representation and reporting within autism research internationally.

articles.title: Not just what happened, but how it felt: Subjective distress and its role in adolescent health after childhood physical abuse
articles.authors: Lia Ferschmann; Else-Marie Augusti; Marte Svartsund Thomassen; Mari Skogseth Fuglesang; Sjur Skjørshammer Sætren; Gertrud Sofie Hafstad
articles.abstract: The role of subjective experience in understanding the links between childhood physical abuse and mental and somatic outcomes is gaining recognition but remains underexplored. Using data from a large population-based sample of youth (12–16 years) and generalized linear models, we examined whether current and past peak subjective distress following physical abuse were associated with symptoms, measured by the Hopkins Symptom Checklist (HSCL-10) and the Children’s Somatic Symptoms Inventory (CSSI-8). Causal mediation analyses were conducted to investigate whether subjective distress mediated the relationship between physical abuse and health outcomes. Subjective distress accounted for variation in symptoms, above and beyond severity and frequency of physical abuse. The impact of physical abuse on health was largely transmitted through subjective distress. While severity and frequency of maltreatment remain independent predictors of health outcomes, this study underscores the necessity of incorporating measures of subjective experience to understand the pathways linking childhood physical abuse to later health outcomes.

articles.title: Alignment between Infant Sleep Advice and Parenting Approach: Associations with Advice Use and Satisfaction in a Cross-Sectional Survey of Australian Parents
articles.authors: Heather Liebregts; Alex Metse; Andrea R. Steele; Kelli Kathleen MacMillan; Rhonda Marriott; Renita Almeida
articles.abstract: Infant sleep is a relational, caregiving experience, yet parents encounter advice about it that varies in how well it fits the way they already care for their infant. How parents engage with this advice may relate to how well it aligns with their usual parenting approach, but this has not been examined. This exploratory study characterised parents' experiences of infant sleep advice from health professionals and other sources and examined whether alignment of advice with parents' usual parenting approach was associated with its use and with satisfaction. An online sample of 201 Western Australian parents (98% female) of an infant aged 0–3 years (mean infant age 16.25 months) rated, for each type of advice received and separately by source, its alignment with their usual way of parenting, whether they had used it, and their satisfaction with outcomes. Complete responsiveness was rated most aligned and used most often; extinction-based approaches least aligned. Health professionals more often provided extinction-based advice and other sources complete responsiveness; 43.5% of parents who received health-professional advice had not sought it. Greater alignment was associated with greater advice use (OR = 3.66 per one point increase in alignment) and higher satisfaction (B = 0.69), more so than type of advice or its source. Results suggest parents' engagement with advice reflects how well it fits their existing parenting approach. Supporting families well may therefore require a broader range of acceptable, relational approaches, attuned to the caregiving relationship rather than to infant behaviour alone.

articles.title: Feasible Cognition Requires Latent State
articles.authors: Ian S. Howard
articles.abstract: Intelligent behavior across motor control, speech production, learning, and social cognition operates under uncertainty: sensory feedback is noisy and delayed, actions are imprecise, and observable outcomes often have ambiguous causes. When multiple latent states generate identical or sufficiently similar observations, regulation, learning, and evaluation based on behavior alone become underdetermined. We argue that inference over latent state is therefore a feasibility condition for cognition under partial observability, rather than merely a modeling convenience. Observable signals—movements, sensory inputs, speech outputs, and social actions—should be understood as noisy evidence about hidden causes, including motor state, articulatory configuration, task context, and intentions. This perspective suggests that separate psychological literatures share a common control-theoretic structure: regulation under noise, delay, ambiguity, and partial observability. It also helps explain why diverse domains exhibit robustness, tolerance of variability, context sensitivity, and structured credit assignment. These properties arise from regulation of inferred, task-relevant state, rather than precise control of observable behavior. The account is not proposed as a replacement for belief-state, internal-model, predictive-coding, or active-inference approaches, but as a cross-domain feasibility argument: latent-state representations support control, learning, and evaluation only when task-relevant hidden distinctions are detectable from observations and stabilizable or actionable. Cognition, from this view, depends on latent state estimates that render behavior, learning, and evaluation well-defined under uncertainty.

articles.title: AI–Human Support Profiles Among Sustained Users of Conversational AI for Emotional Support in China: A Latent Profile Analysis
articles.authors: Rong Fu; Jiasheng Huang
articles.abstract:
Background: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for emotional support. Among sustained users, AI may become an enduring part of their broader support ecology rather than a one-off or short-term coping strategy, yet little is known about how AI and human support are configured within this population.
Objective: This study aimed to identify AI–human support profiles among sustained users of conversational AI for emotional support in China and compare their AI use, satisfaction, psychological distress, and positive well-being.
Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 484 individuals who had used conversational AI for emotional support at least once per week for more than 1 continuous month were recruited online between February and March 2026, with sustained use verified through uploaded conversation screenshots. Latent profile analysis was conducted using perceived emotional support and emotional closeness from AI and human sources, and differences in AI use, satisfaction, and psychological outcomes were compared across profiles.
Results: Participants were on average 23.62 years old (SD 4.24), and 59.3% (287/484) were women. A 3-profile solution was retained (entropy=0.824): human-anchored integrated (221/484, 45.7%), AI–human divergent (167/484, 34.5%), and AI-compensatory (96/484, 19.8%). The profiles were characterized by strong human resources with substantial AI support, greater perceived support from AI than from humans despite greater human closeness, and moderate AI support with near-floor human support, respectively. Profile differences were larger for human support and closeness (partial η²=.878 and .868) than for AI support and closeness (partial η²=.058 and .010). General-purpose AI systems predominated, and no significant profile differences existed in system type or most use behaviors. Significant profile differences existed in total AI use time (P=.019) and satisfaction (P=.013), with the AI–human divergent profile using AI longer but reporting lower satisfaction than the human-anchored integrated profile. No significant differences existed in depression, anxiety, perceived stress, or loneliness (all P≥.050). Significant differences existed in life satisfaction (P=.008) and subjective happiness (P<.001), with the human-anchored integrated profile reporting the highest positive well-being.
Conclusions: These findings highlight heterogeneity in how AI and human support are configured within sustained users’ broader support ecologies and suggest that human-anchored integration is associated with more favorable positive well-being, despite broadly similar AI use behaviors and psychological symptom levels across profiles.

articles.title: Straight-line behavior: conforming to design in a practice environment
articles.authors: Jordan Gutterman; Gillian Gold; Peter Brusilovsky; Paulo F. Carvalho
articles.abstract: Practice is an important component of computer science education, and online learning platforms increasingly provide students with large collections of programming examples and activities. How do students navigate among available practice opportunities when choosing what to work on next? Using interaction data from 247 students across three undergraduate computer science courses, we investigate the tendency for students to select the next programming activity as presented in the system, conforming to the implied sequence presented by a learning interface, which we call “straight-line behavior.” Students become less likely to follow the displayed sequence as a session progresses, while they are slightly more likely to continue in sequence following programming practice activities than example-based activities. Finally, students with more straight-line behavior also complete larger portions of the available programming curriculum. These findings suggest that both the organization of learning opportunities within educational interfaces and the decisions of how to structure curricula might contribute to their learning experiences. While adherence to displayed learning sequences may be an overlooked dimension of student behavior in computer science learning environments, it may offer opportunities for designing systems to account for differences in how students navigate programming practice.

articles.title: Why You Switch Matters: Failure-Triggered Switching Between Different Problem Types is More Related to Programming Performance than General Switching
articles.authors: Pragati Maheshwary; Gillian Gold; Jordan Barria-Pineda; Peter Brusilovsky; Paulo F. Carvalho
articles.abstract: The increasing adoption of self-directed programming practice environments creates new opportunities to examine how learners regulate their use of instructional supports and how these decisions influence learning outcomes. In this study, we analyze fine-grained log data from 115 students enrolled in an introductory programming course to investigate learners’ preferences and transitions between scaffolded tasks (e.g., tracing and code completion problems), code writing tasks, and worked examples. Using problem-level regression analyses, we investigate how prior knowledge, recent performance, and use of examples relate to learners’ regulatory decisions and subsequent performance outcomes. We found that higher prior knowledge was associated with higher success rates and productive struggle. Additionally, students with higher pretest scores were also slightly more likely to transition between task types. In general, switching behavior was symmetric: students were equally likely to move from code writing to scaffolded tasks as from scaffolded tasks to coding. However, failure on the prior problem significantly increased the likelihood of switching, and failure-triggered switching was positively associated with success, suggesting that why learners switch matters more than whether they switch task types. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating both learner characteristics and recent performance signals into self-regulated sequencing decisions. Productive practice may depend not only on the completed problems, but also on how learners adapt in response to failure, providing suggestions for programming environments that support strategic sequencing.

articles.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Promote Metacognition? Evidence from a Three-Level Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Xiuya Li; Xiaowen Liu; Lei Heya; Haibo Yang
articles.abstract: With the rapid advancement of digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from early intelligent tutoring systems to contemporary generative AI. Although AI features—such as personalization, adaptability, and instant feedback—have the potential to facilitate learners’ metacognition, empirical findings regarding the effectiveness of AI remain inconclusive. To address this gap, the present study employed a three-level meta-analysis of 54 studies (k = 121; N = 7,431) to examine the effects of AI interventions on metacognition. The results revealed a significant positive effect of AI on metacognition (Hedges’ g = 0.624, SE = 0.099, p < .001, 95% CI [0.431, 0.817]). Moderator analyses demonstrated that the control condition, intervention duration, and data source significantly moderated this effect, whereas other study, methodological, participant, and AI characteristics did not. These findings quantify the overall impact of AI on metacognition and identify key boundary conditions, thereby providing valuable insights for future research and educational practice.

articles.title: Profiling the Chinese Participants in Psychological Science: Non-WEIRD but Not Representative
articles.authors: Lei Yue; Zhangweiwei; Chunxiao Wang; Xi-Nian Zuo; Hu Chuan-Peng
articles.abstract: Psychological science aims at understanding the human mind and behavior, but it primarily relies on participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic regions, i.e., the WEIRD problem. This lack of diversity and representativeness of participants compromises the generalizability of psychological science. To address this issue, large-scale international collaborative projects have been initiated, and more data have been collected from non-WEIRD regions. However, it is unknown whether participants from non-WEIRD regions can represent their local population. In this preregistered report, we depicted the demographic profile of Chinese participants reported in 1, 000 empirical studies (n = 554, 794) published in five mainstream Chinese psychological journals and in 27 large-scale international collaborative projects (n = 29, 006, accounting for 2.12% of all participants). We found that age and sex were the most reported demographic variables, and other aspects of participants were less reported. The available demographic information revealed that Chinese participants were not representative of the population: most were young, well-educated, and resided in East China. Also, Chinese participants in large-scale international collaborative projects are less representative than those from Chinese journals in terms of geographical distributions. The demographic profile of Chinese participants in psychology is similar to their counterparts in many other countries and regions, suggesting the globalization of young and highly educated participants in psychological science. Together, our findings indicate that problems of representativeness are deeply entrenched in global psychological science and require coordinated cross-sector efforts.

articles.title: A General Neural Network Approach for Fitting and Comparing Attentional Decision-Making Models
articles.authors: Bingsong Zhao; Peter D. Kvam
articles.abstract: Attentional decision models (ADMs), including attention-modulated decision models and joint models of attention and decision making, are important tools for studying the cognitive processes underlying decision formation. However, these models often cannot be fit or compared using likelihood-based methods. Building on simulation-based and machine-learning approaches, this paper develops and tests an end-to-end neural network framework for parameter estimation and model comparison, tailored to the high-dimensional, multimodal structure of attentional decision data.  In attentional drift diffusion models where likelihood-based fitting is feasible, we compared machine-learning methods to likelihood-based methods on parameter recovery, model recovery, and empirical data fitting. The machine-learning approach performed as well or better than the likelihood-based approach. The two methods yielded highly consistent conclusions for real participants on these tasks. In more complex models where likelihood-based methods are inapplicable, the machine-learning approach still achieved high accuracy in parameter recovery and model recovery. Moreover, we compared different feature-extraction strategies and network architectures and found that even the simplest were sufficient for reliable estimation and comparison with large-scale simulation data. Overall, our approach provides practical methodological tools that facilitate the advancement of attentional decision models and the development of associated theories.

articles.title: Is the Future Modular? Mapping Preferences, Benefits, and Risks of Modular Journalism across three Audience Segments
articles.authors: Sophie Morosoli; Hannes Cools; Natali Helberger
articles.abstract: One of the ways in which GenAI could change the future of news is modular journalism (MJ) – presenting news in novel, more fluid, personalized and interactive formats that respond and adjust to the individual preferences of users. Being more responsive to users' individual needs through AI-supported forms of personalization could unlock new ways of catering to diverse or underserved audiences, and potentially even reduce news avoidance and information overload or serve as the foundation for new news experiences. This study investigates audience evaluations and willingness to pay for MJ through focus groups (N=26) with three diverse user segments: basic subscribers, adolescents, and individuals with migration backgrounds. Findings reveal that particularly young adults and individuals with migration backgrounds are interested in MJ, valuing flexibility and engagement, though concerns exist about oversimplification of serious topics.
